pharsalus.t: Thessalian city of Phthiotis, long ruled by aristocratic families, whose plain saw Caesar's victory over Pompey in 48 BCE.
pharsalus.o: Pharsalus stood on a hill above the plain of the Enipeus in southern Thessaly, in the region Greek myth linked to Achilles's Phthia. It became a city in the Archaic period and one of the leading members of the Thessalian League with Larissa and Pherae.
pharsalus.r: Pharsalus was dominated by aristocratic families such as the Echecratidae. In the 370s BCE Polydamas governed the city and was forced to submit to Jason of Pherae. Daochus, a Pharsalian, served Philip II as tetrarch of Thessaly and set up a family monument at Delphi.
pharsalus.e: Pharsalus passed under Macedonian rule, was freed by Rome in 196 BCE and came under Roman control by 146 BCE. In 48 BCE Julius Caesar defeated Pompey nearby at the Battle of Pharsalus.

principality-of-achaea.t: Most successful crusader state in Greece, a French chivalric society in the Peloponnese whose story is told in the Chronicle of the Morea.
principality-of-achaea.o: In 1205 William of Champlitte and Geoffrey of Villehardouin, crusaders of the Fourth Crusade, conquered the western Peloponnese after defeating local Greeks at the Olive Grove of Koundouros. Geoffrey I took control after Champlitte left, and his family ruled for three generations under the nominal suzerainty of the Latin Empire.
principality-of-achaea.r: The principality was a model feudal state, divided into twelve baronies, such as Karytaina, Akova and Patras, whose lords sat in the prince's council. Its laws were codified as the Assizes of Romania. The court at Andravida and the port of Clarentza were famed for French culture, and the castle of Chlemoutsi guarded the coast. Greek archons kept their lands.
principality-of-achaea.e: Captured at Pelagonia in 1259, William II of Villehardouin ceded Mistras and Monemvasia to Byzantium, creating the base of the Despotate of the Morea. Angevin, Navarrese and Zaccaria rulers followed. Thomas Palaiologos annexed the rest of the principality in 1430-1432.

principality-of-masserano.t: A tiny papal fief in northern Piedmont ruled by the Ferrero-Fieschi family until it was sold to the kings of Sardinia in 1767.
principality-of-masserano.o: Masserano and Crevacuore, small towns in the hills between Biella and the Sesia valley, belonged to the Fieschi family and then to the Ferrero, who took the Fieschi name. In 1598 Pope Clement VIII raised them to a principality held as a fief of the Holy See, giving the family sovereign status.
principality-of-masserano.r: The Ferrero-Fieschi princes governed a few thousand subjects, minted coins and kept a small court, while often serving foreign rulers as soldiers and diplomats, especially Spain. Surrounded by the Duchy of Savoy, the state survived through papal protection and its rulers' connections abroad. Little else is recorded of its government.
principality-of-masserano.e: The House of Savoy, now kings of the Kingdom of Sardinia, long sought to absorb the enclave. In 1767 the prince ceded his sovereignty to Charles Emmanuel III, ending the principality.

praisos.t: East Cretan city of the Eteocretans, a pre-Greek people whose language survives in a few undeciphered inscriptions.
praisos.o: Praisos stood on hills in the interior of eastern Crete. Herodotus and Strabo say its people were Eteocretans, 'true Cretans' descended from the island's pre-Greek inhabitants, and the settlement continued from the end of the Bronze Age into the Iron Age.
praisos.r: Inscriptions from Praisos, written in the Greek alphabet between the 6th and 3rd centuries BCE, record a non-Greek language that remains undeciphered. The city controlled the sanctuary of Diktaean Zeus for a time and quarrelled with Itanos. It had harbours on both coasts of eastern Crete.
praisos.e: Praisos was destroyed by its neighbour Hierapytna c. 145 BCE, which took over its land. Its inscriptions are the main evidence for the Eteocretan language.
praisos.re: Cretan religion; cult of Diktaean Zeus

principality-of-boisbelle.t: A sovereign enclave in Berry, exempt from royal taxes, where Henry IV's minister Sully built the planned town of Henrichemont.
principality-of-boisbelle.o: Boisbelle was a lordship in Berry whose holders had long claimed sovereignty, a privilege tolerated by the French crown. In 1597 Maximilien de Béthune, later duke of Sully, Henry IV's chief minister, bought it and confirmed its status as a principality.
principality-of-boisbelle.r: Sully founded the town of Henrichemont in 1608, named after the king, on a regular grid around a central square, hoping to attract Protestant settlers and artisans. Its inhabitants paid no royal taxes, which drew some settlers, though the town never grew as planned. The Béthune family ruled the enclave for over 150 years.
principality-of-boisbelle.e: In 1766 the Duke of Sully's descendants sold the principality to Louis XV, ending its sovereignty, and it became part of the Kingdom of France.
ru: Maximilien de Béthune, Duke of Sully

principality-of-bari.t: A short-lived Lombard principality carved out of Norman Apulia by a local strongman before Roger II brought it to heel.
principality-of-bari.o: In the weak reign of Duke William II of the Duchy of Apulia and Calabria, the citizen Grimoald Alferanites took power in Bari in 1119 and called himself prince. Bari, the old seat of Byzantine government in Italy, had since 1087 housed the relics of Saint Nicholas, which made it a major pilgrimage centre.
principality-of-bari.r: Little is known of Grimoald's government beyond his alliances with Venice and with other rebellious Apulian barons. He relied on Bari's port, its merchant community and the prestige of the Basilica of San Nicola. He submitted to Roger II of Sicily in 1129 when Roger took over Apulia.
principality-of-bari.e: Grimoald joined a baronial revolt against Roger II, who captured Bari in 1132 and sent him as a prisoner to Sicily. Bari was absorbed into the Kingdom of Sicily.

provisional-government-of-milan.t: The government formed by the Milanese after the Five Days of 1848 drove out the Austrians, which merged Lombardy with Piedmont before Radetzky returned.
provisional-government-of-milan.o: From 18 to 22 March 1848 the people of Milan fought the Five Days, barricade battles that forced Marshal Radetzky's Austrian garrison to leave the city. A provisional government headed by the mayor Gabrio Casati took power, while the democrat Carlo Cattaneo led the council of war during the fighting.
provisional-government-of-milan.r: The provisional government governed Lombardy and called on Charles Albert of the Kingdom of Sardinia, who declared war on Austria. Moderates led by Casati favoured union with Piedmont, while republicans such as Cattaneo and Giuseppe Mazzini wanted to delay the question. A plebiscite in May and June approved fusion with Piedmont.
provisional-government-of-milan.e: After the Piedmontese defeat at Custoza in July 1848, Radetzky reoccupied Milan on 6 August, and Lombardy returned to the Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia.

principality-of-the-hevelli.t: A Slavic principality on the Havel centred on Brandenburg, whose last prince bequeathed his land to Albert the Bear and so began the March of Brandenburg.
principality-of-the-hevelli.o: The Hevelli, also called Stodorani, were West Slavic settlers of the Havel lands west of modern Berlin from the 7th or 8th century. Their chief stronghold was Brenna, the later Brandenburg an der Havel. In 928 to 929 the East Frankish king Henry the Fowler captured it in winter across the frozen marshes.
principality-of-the-hevelli.r: The Hevelli were governed by princes from Brenna, controlling river crossings and fortified settlements on the Havel and Spree. German rule after 929 was lost in the Great Slav Rising of 983, and the Hevelli joined, and later stood apart from, the Lutician Federation. The last prince, Pribislav-Henry, became a Christian and ruled as a German ally.
principality-of-the-hevelli.e: Pribislav-Henry named Albert the Bear his heir; on his death in 1150 Albert took Brandenburg, securing it in 1157 after a fight with the Slavic prince Jaxa of Köpenick. The Hevelli lands became the core of the Margraviate of Brandenburg.

parthenopean-republic.t: The Neapolitan republic of 1799, whose idealistic leaders were crushed by Cardinal Ruffo's peasant army and executed in their hundreds.
parthenopean-republic.o: After the Kingdom of Naples attacked the French in Rome in late 1798 and was defeated, King Ferdinand IV fled to Sicily. French troops under General Championnet fought their way into Naples, and on 23 January 1799 local patriots proclaimed a republic named after Parthenope, the ancient Greek name for the city.
parthenopean-republic.r: The republic was led by intellectuals and liberal nobles such as Carlo Lauberg and the jurist Francesco Mario Pagano, who drafted a constitution. Eleonora Fonseca Pimentel edited its newspaper, the Monitore Napoletano. It tried to abolish feudalism, but had little support among the poor and peasants, and depended on French troops, who withdrew in May.
parthenopean-republic.e: Cardinal Fabrizio Ruffo's Sanfedisti army retook Naples in June 1799. The surrender terms were broken with Nelson's backing, and over a hundred republicans, including Pagano, Pimentel and Admiral Francesco Caracciolo, were executed.

perinthus.t: Samian colony on the Sea of Marmara that, with Byzantium, defeated Philip II's siege of 340 BCE.
perinthus.o: Colonists from Samos founded Perinthus c. 602 BCE on a promontory on the north shore of the Propontis, in Thrace. They soon fought off attacks by Megarian settlers from neighbouring colonies.
perinthus.r: Perinthus traded with the Thracian interior and along the Propontis route to Byzantium. It resisted the Persian general Megabazus c. 512 BCE but was conquered. Later it paid tribute in the Delian League. In 340 BCE Philip II besieged the city with towers and rams, but Persian satraps and Byzantium helped it hold out.
perinthus.e: Perinthus kept its independence under Hellenistic kings and the Odrysian Kingdom's influence. When Rome made Thrace a province in 46 CE, it became the provincial capital, later renamed Heraclea; it is modern Marmara Ereğlisi.

principality-of-samos.t: Autonomous Christian principality on the island of Samos under Ottoman suzerainty, created after the Greek War of Independence and united with Greece in 1912.
principality-of-samos.o: Samos fought in the Greek War of Independence, but the London Protocol of 1830 left it outside the new Greek state. As a compromise the Ottoman Sultan made it an autonomous principality, established in 1834, with a Christian prince appointed by the Porte and paying an annual tribute. Its first prince was Stefanos Vogoridis.
principality-of-samos.r: The prince, usually a Phanariot Greek, governed with an elected assembly and his own administration, flag and later postage stamps, from Vathy. Samians paid low taxes and enjoyed religious freedom. The economy rested on wine, especially muscat, tobacco and shipping. Politics were often turbulent, with clashes between princes and local factions.
principality-of-samos.e: During the First Balkan War, the Samian leader Themistoklis Sofoulis drove out the last Ottoman garrison and the assembly declared union with Greece in November 1912. Greek rule was confirmed in 1913 and Samos joined the Kingdom of Greece.

palace-state-of-phaistos.t: Minoan palace centre of the Mesara plain in southern Crete, famous for its grand staircases and the enigmatic Phaistos Disc.
palace-state-of-phaistos.o: Phaistos stands on a ridge above the Mesara, the largest plain of Crete, which had been settled since the Neolithic. Around 1950 BCE its first palace was built around a paved central court, and Phaistos became the leading power of southern Crete. After destructions in the 18th century BCE the palace was rebuilt on a grander scale.
palace-state-of-phaistos.r: Phaistos controlled the agricultural wealth of the Mesara and probably the nearby port of Kommos, which traded with Egypt and the Levant. Its archives of clay sealings and Linear A tablets reveal a developed palace bureaucracy. Finds include fine Kamares ware pottery and the stamped clay Phaistos Disc, whose script is still undeciphered. The nearby villa of Ayia Triada was closely linked to it.
palace-state-of-phaistos.e: The palace was destroyed c. 1450 BCE and its role passed largely to Ayia Triada and to Knossos, which came to dominate Crete under Mycenaean rulers. Phaistos later revived as a Greek city-state, described separately as Phaistos. The site was excavated by Italian archaeologists from 1900.

prince-bishopric-of-halberstadt.t: Church principality in the northern Harz foreland, founded under Charlemagne and secularised to Brandenburg at the Peace of Westphalia.
prince-bishopric-of-halberstadt.o: The diocese of Halberstadt was founded about 804 under Charlemagne to christianise the eastern Saxons. Its bishops gathered counties and estates in the Harz foreland. After the fall of Henry the Lion in 1180 freed them from his ducal power, they ruled a consolidated territory as imperial princes.
prince-bishopric-of-halberstadt.r: The cathedral chapter elected the bishop, who ruled from Halberstadt and towns such as Gröningen. Its Gothic cathedral and treasury are among the richest in Germany. From the 16th century the see was held by princes of the houses of Brandenburg and Brunswick, including Albert of Brandenburg and Henry Julius of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, and the territory became Lutheran. In the Thirty Years War its administrator, Christian of Brunswick, fought for the Protestant side.
prince-bishopric-of-halberstadt.e: At the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 the see was secularised and given to Brandenburg as the Principality of Halberstadt. It remained Prussian, apart from the Kingdom of Westphalia interlude, and is now in Saxony-Anhalt.

principality-of-catalonia.t: The union of Catalan counties under the House of Barcelona, a land of parliaments, merchant cities and its own laws within the Crown of Aragon.
principality-of-catalonia.o: Catalonia grew out of the counties of the Marca Hispanica, gradually gathered under the County of Barcelona. In 1162 Alfonso II inherited both Barcelona and the Kingdom of Aragon, and the Catalan counties became one constituent of the Crown of Aragon. The name Principality became usual in the 14th century.
principality-of-catalonia.r: Catalonia was governed under the Usatges of Barcelona and its Corts, whose standing committee, the Generalitat, was created in 1359. Barcelona's merchants traded across the Mediterranean under the Consulate of the Sea. Catalan literature flourished with Ramon Llull and Ausiàs March, while the Black Death and civil war of 1462-1472 brought decline.
principality-of-catalonia.e: The Reapers' War of 1640 led to the loss of Roussillon to France in 1659. Siding with the Habsburg claimant in the War of the Spanish Succession, Barcelona fell in 1714, and the Nueva Planta decree of 1716 abolished Catalonia's institutions.

prince-bishopric-of-chur.t: Alpine church state ruled by the bishops of Chur, one of the oldest sees north of the Alps, whose temporal power was broken by the leagues of Graubünden.
prince-bishopric-of-chur.o: A bishop of Chur is recorded in 451, making it one of the oldest dioceses north of the Alps. Carolingian and Ottonian kings granted the bishops immunities, tolls and lands in Rhaetia, controlling routes to the Alpine passes. In 1170 Emperor Frederick Barbarossa raised the bishop to the rank of an imperial prince, giving the church a recognised secular principality.
prince-bishopric-of-chur.r: The bishops governed estates in the Rhine valley, the Engadine and the Vinschgau from their court in Chur, with officials in castles along the pass roads. Romansh, German and Lombard dialects were all spoken in their lands. To resist episcopal power, the subjects formed the League of God's House in 1367, which later joined the Grey League and the League of the Ten Jurisdictions in the Three Leagues.
prince-bishopric-of-chur.e: The Ilanz Articles of 1524 and 1526 stripped the bishop of most secular authority and handed it to the communes of the Three Leagues. The bishops kept a few rights and the title of prince until 1803, and the Catholic diocese of Chur continues today.

phocaea.t: Ionian city whose daring sailors founded Massalia and explored the western Mediterranean as far as Tartessos in Spain.
phocaea.o: Phocaea, the northernmost Ionian city, was founded on a peninsula north of the Hermus c. 1000 BCE by settlers said to have come from Phocis. Its rocky territory pushed the Phocaeans to the sea, and from the 7th century BCE they sailed long distances in fast fifty-oared ships.
phocaea.r: Herodotus credits Phocaeans with opening the Adriatic, Tyrrhenian and Iberian seas. They founded Lampsacus, Massalia c. 600 BCE, Alalia on Corsica and Emporion in Spain, and won the friendship of King Arganthonius of Tartessos. When Harpagus besieged the city c. 545 BCE, most citizens sailed west; those at Alalia fought Carthaginians and Etruscans c. 540 BCE.
phocaea.e: Phocaea recovered and provided Dionysius, commander of the Greek fleet at Lade in 494 BCE. In 132 BCE it backed Aristonicus against Rome and was spared destruction only through Massalia's appeal, then joined the province of Asia.

principality-of-sedan.t: A Protestant sovereign principality on the Meuse, ruled by the La Marck and La Tour d'Auvergne families, which sheltered Huguenots and French rebels.
principality-of-sedan.o: In 1424 Everard de la Marck acquired the lordship of Sedan on the Meuse, at the frontier between France, Luxembourg and Liège. His descendants built a great fortress there and claimed sovereignty, owing allegiance to neither the French king nor the emperor.
principality-of-sedan.r: Robert II de la Marck and his successors were also dukes of Bouillon. The princes adopted Calvinism, and Sedan became a Huguenot refuge with a Protestant academy founded in 1602. In 1591 the heiress Charlotte de la Marck married Henri de La Tour d'Auvergne, father of Marshal Turenne, who was born at Sedan in 1611. Sedan's cloth industry later flourished.
principality-of-sedan.e: Frédéric-Maurice de La Tour d'Auvergne joined the conspiracy of Cinq-Mars against Richelieu, and to save his life ceded Sedan to Louis XIII in 1642. The principality was absorbed into the Kingdom of France.
ru: Henri de La Tour d'Auvergne, Duke of Bouillon

praeneste.t: Latin hill city east of Rome, famous for its princely tombs, its bronze cistae and the oracle of Fortuna Primigenia.
praeneste.o: Praeneste, modern Palestrina, occupied a spur of the Monti Prenestini commanding the routes from Latium to Campania. In the 7th century BCE its rulers were buried in the Bernardini and Barberini tombs with gold, silver and ivory from the eastern Mediterranean, among the richest burials in Italy.
praeneste.r: Praeneste was a powerful and often independent member of the Latin League. Its workshops produced engraved bronze cistae, cylindrical boxes for toiletries such as the Ficoroni cista. The sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia, where oracles were drawn by lot, was later rebuilt on a vast terraced scale in the 2nd century BCE. Local Latin had distinct features noted by Roman writers.
praeneste.e: Praeneste fought Rome in the Latin War and lost land in 338 BCE, but remained a separate allied city until it gained citizenship after the Social War. It sheltered Gaius Marius the Younger in 82 BCE; Sulla took it, executed its men and planted a colony.

plataea.t: Small Boeotian city that defied Thebes, stood with Athens at Marathon and gave its name to the battle that ended the Persian invasion of Greece in 479 BCE.
plataea.o: Plataea lay on the northern slopes of Mount Cithaeron, on the border between Boeotia and Attica. When Thebes pressed it to join the Boeotian League in the late 6th century BCE, the Plataeans turned to Athens, traditionally in 519 BCE. That alliance shaped the rest of their history: alone among the Greeks, they sent their whole levy to fight beside the Athenians at Marathon in 490 BCE.
plataea.r: A modest farming community governed by its own citizen assembly, Plataea mattered far beyond its size. In 479 BCE the allied Greek army under the Spartan Pausanias defeated the Persian general Mardonius on its territory, and the city was charged with tending the graves of the fallen and hosting a festival of freedom, the Eleutheria. Its people spoke the Boeotian dialect and kept close cultural ties with Athens.
plataea.e: Theban aggression began the Peloponnesian War at Plataea in 431 BCE; after a famous siege the city surrendered to Sparta and was razed in 427 BCE. Restored in 386 BCE, it was destroyed again by Thebes in 373 BCE and rebuilt under Philip II and Alexander. It then belonged to the Boeotian League until Roman conquest in 146 BCE.

principality-of-nassau-diez.t: Nassau territory on the Lahn whose counts, as hereditary stadtholders of Friesland, became the House of Orange-Nassau that rules the Netherlands today.
principality-of-nassau-diez.o: Nassau-Diez arose in the 1606 partition of the lands of John VI of Nassau-Dillenburg, when Ernst Casimir received Diez on the Lahn. Ernst Casimir served the Dutch Republic as a general and became stadtholder of Friesland and Groningen, beginning his line's long connection with the northern Netherlands.
principality-of-nassau-diez.r: The German lands were small and governed from Diez and later the Oranienstein palace, while the counts spent their careers in the Dutch Republic, where they held the Frisian stadtholdership hereditarily. They were raised to princes of the Empire in 1654. John William Friso inherited part of William III's Orange claims in 1702, and his son William IV united all Nassau-Ottonian lands by 1743.
principality-of-nassau-diez.e: William IV became stadtholder of all the United Provinces in 1747. In 1806 Napoleon confiscated the German lands, which went to the Grand Duchy of Berg, and after 1815 they passed to the Duchy of Nassau and Prussia. William IV's grandson became King William I of the Netherlands.

paris-commune.t: The revolutionary government that ruled Paris for ten weeks in 1871, and whose bloody suppression became a lasting symbol for the socialist left.
paris-commune.o: After France's defeat by Prussia and the long siege of Paris, the government of Adolphe Thiers tried to remove the National Guard's cannons from Montmartre on 18 March 1871. Parisians resisted, the government withdrew to Versailles, and elections on 26 March created the Commune.
paris-commune.r: The Commune's council, a mix of Jacobins, socialists and followers of Proudhon and Blanqui, separated church and state, abolished night work in bakeries, let workers take over abandoned workshops and postponed rents. Women such as Louise Michel played prominent roles. The Communards also pulled down the Vendôme Column.
paris-commune.e: Government troops entered Paris on 21 May, and during the 'Bloody Week' that followed thousands of Communards were killed, many by summary execution; the Communards shot hostages and burned the Tuileries. Thousands more were tried and deported to New Caledonia. The French Third Republic survived.

principality-of-dombes.t: A small sovereign principality north of Lyon, with its own parliament and mint at Trévoux, held by royal relatives until it was sold to Louis XV.
principality-of-dombes.o: The Dombes, a plateau of ponds east of the Saône, belonged to the lords of Beaujeu and then the dukes of Bourbon. After the confiscation of the Constable of Bourbon's lands in 1523 it was held by the crown, then restored in 1560 to the Bourbon-Montpensier family, who ruled it as a sovereign principality outside the Kingdom of France.
principality-of-dombes.r: The princes kept a parliament at Trévoux, minted coin and taxed separately, though in practice the land was closely tied to France. Anne Marie Louise d'Orléans, La Grande Mademoiselle, held it and in 1681 ceded it to the Duke of Maine, Louis XIV's legitimised son. Jesuits at Trévoux published the Journal de Trévoux and the Dictionnaire de Trévoux.
principality-of-dombes.e: In 1762 the Duke of Maine's son, the Count of Eu, exchanged the principality with Louis XV for lands in France, and it became part of the kingdom.

priene.t: Small Ionian city near Mount Mycale, home of the sage Bias and later rebuilt as the best-preserved example of a Hellenistic grid-planned town.
priene.o: Priene was one of the twelve Ionian cities, founded by tradition by settlers from Athens and Thebes c. 1000 BCE. Its original site near the Maeander has never been found. The Panionion, the common sanctuary of the Ionian League on Mount Mycale, lay in its territory, giving Priene a role in Ionian affairs out of proportion to its size.
priene.r: In the 6th century BCE Bias of Priene, counted among the Seven Sages, advised the Ionians to emigrate to Sardinia rather than submit to Persia. Priene fell to the Kingdom of Lydia and then the Achaemenid Empire, sent 12 ships to the Battle of Lade in 494 BCE and later paid tribute in the Delian League.
priene.e: In the mid-4th century BCE the city was rebuilt on a terrace of Mycale with a strict grid; Alexander dedicated its temple of Athena Polias. It passed to Rome in 133 BCE. As the Maeander silted its harbour, Priene declined, leaving its ruins remarkably intact.
priene.re: Greek religion; cult of Athena Polias

provisional-government-of-the-french-rep.t: The government that restored the Republic after liberation, gave French women the vote and built the post-war welfare state.
provisional-government-of-the-french-rep.o: In June 1944 the French Committee of National Liberation in Algiers renamed itself the Provisional Government of the French Republic, led by Charles de Gaulle. After Paris was liberated in August 1944, it moved to the capital and declared that Vichy France had never been legitimate.
provisional-government-of-the-french-rep.r: The government included Gaullists, communists, socialists and Christian democrats from the Resistance. Women voted for the first time in 1945. It nationalised Renault, coal, electricity and major banks, created the social security system and the Monnet Plan for reconstruction, and oversaw the trials of collaborators. France gained a seat on the UN Security Council and an occupation zone in Germany.
provisional-government-of-the-french-rep.e: De Gaulle resigned in January 1946 over disputes about the constitution, and Félix Gouin and Georges Bidault led the government. After a first draft was rejected, voters approved a new constitution in October 1946, founding the French Fourth Republic.

prince-bishopric-of-wurzburg.t: Franconian church state whose bishops styled themselves Dukes of Franconia and built one of Europe's grandest baroque palaces, the Würzburg Residenz.
prince-bishopric-of-wurzburg.o: The diocese was founded in 742 by Saint Boniface, with Burkard as its first bishop. Royal grants gave the bishops wide lands on the Main, and in 1168 Emperor Frederick Barbarossa confirmed their judicial and ducal rights across eastern Franconia, the basis of their later title of Dukes of Franconia and of a territorial principality inside the Holy Roman Empire.
prince-bishopric-of-wurzburg.r: The prince-bishop was elected by the noble cathedral chapter and governed from the Marienberg fortress, later from the town below. Julius Echter von Mespelbrunn refounded the university in 1582, built the Juliusspital and drove a forceful Counter-Reformation. The 17th century saw some of Germany's worst witch trials. Under the Schönborn bishops Balthasar Neumann built the Residenz, decorated with Tiepolo's ceiling frescoes, and vineyards along the Main supported a wealthy wine trade.
prince-bishopric-of-wurzburg.e: Secularised in 1802 and given to Bavaria, the territory became the Grand Duchy of Würzburg under Ferdinand of Tuscany from 1805 to 1814 before returning to the Kingdom of Bavaria. The diocese survives, and the Residenz is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

prince-bishopric-of-minden.t: Weser valley church state founded after Charlemagne's Saxon wars and secularised into a Brandenburg principality in 1648.
prince-bishopric-of-minden.o: The diocese of Minden was founded around 800 after Charlemagne's conquest of the Saxons, on a crossing of the Weser. Its bishops gained counties and immunities from the Ottonian and Salian kings. After Henry the Lion fell in 1180 they ruled a territory along the Weser as imperial princes, though Minden itself grew increasingly self-governing.
prince-bishopric-of-minden.r: The cathedral chapter elected the bishops, who often lived at Petershagen because of friction with Minden's citizens. Their land was small, rural and hemmed in by neighbours such as the counties of Schaumburg, Ravensberg and Hoya. The city of Minden adopted Lutheranism in 1530, and in the later 16th century the see was held by Lutheran princes of the houses of Brunswick-Lüneburg and Schaumburg.
prince-bishopric-of-minden.e: At the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 the see was secularised as the Principality of Minden and given to Brandenburg. It remained Prussian, apart from the Napoleonic period, and the town is now in North Rhine-Westphalia.

paeligni.t: Sabellic people of the Abruzzo mountains whose town Corfinium became the rebel capital of the Social War and whose Sulmo was Ovid's birthplace.
paeligni.o: The Paeligni lived in the upland basin of the Aterno and Gizio rivers in central Abruzzo, surrounded by the Marsi, Vestini and Samnites, from the early 1st millennium BCE. Ancient writers counted them among the Sabellian peoples descended from the Sabines, and they spoke a dialect close to Oscan.
paeligni.r: Their main towns were Corfinium, Sulmo and Superaequum, small hill communities that formed a league. Inscriptions in the Paelignian dialect, many in Latin letters, record local gods and priestesses. They kept sheep and controlled routes through the Apennines between Rome and the Adriatic.
paeligni.e: The Paeligni made peace and an alliance with Rome in 304 BCE, together with the Marsi and Marrucini. In 91 BCE they joined the Italian revolt, and Corfinium was renamed Italia as the capital of the rebel confederation. After the Social War they received citizenship; the poet Ovid was born at Sulmo in 43 BCE.

patriarchate-of-aquileia.t: A church principality in Friuli whose patriarchs ruled as imperial princes for over three centuries and whose parliament was among Europe's earliest.
patriarchate-of-aquileia.o: During the Investiture Controversy, Emperor Henry IV rewarded Patriarch Sigehard of Aquileia for his loyalty by granting him the county of Friuli in 1077, soon followed by Istria and Carniola. The patriarchs thus became temporal princes of the Holy Roman Empire, heirs to one of the oldest bishoprics in the Latin West.
patriarchate-of-aquileia.r: Patriarchs, usually German nobles in the early centuries and later Italians or Frenchmen, ruled from Aquileia, Cividale and from the 13th century mainly Udine. The Parliament of Friuli, bringing together clergy, nobles and towns, voted taxes and troops. The principality was constantly squeezed by the counts of Gorizia, the Duchy of Austria and the Republic of Venice; Patriarch Bertrand was murdered by Friulian nobles in 1350.
patriarchate-of-aquileia.e: Venice conquered Friuli in 1420, ending the patriarchs' temporal rule; a settlement in 1445 left them only a few towns. The patriarchate continued as a church office until 1751, when Pope Benedict XIV divided it into the archdioceses of Udine and Gorizia.

prince-bishopric-of-liege.t: A church principality on the Meuse that lasted eight centuries, grew rich on coal and arms making, and balanced its bishops against assertive townspeople.
prince-bishopric-of-liege.o: Bishop Notger (972–1008) gathered secular rights from the Ottonian emperors, including the county of Huy in 985, and turned the see of Liège into a territorial principality of the Holy Roman Empire. He rebuilt the city and its schools, and Liège became one of the leading intellectual centres of the empire.
prince-bishopric-of-liege.r: The prince-bishops shared power with the cathedral chapter and towns; the Peace of Fexhe of 1316 required the consent of the estates for major decisions. Liège mined coal from the 12th century and became famous for metalwork and weapons. Charles the Bold sacked the city in 1468. Erard de la Marck rebuilt it in the early 16th century, and the principality kept a careful neutrality.
prince-bishopric-of-liege.e: The Liège Revolution of 1789 drove out the prince-bishop and created the Republic of Liège; Austrian troops restored him in 1791. French armies annexed the principality in 1795, and its lands were later divided between Belgium and the Netherlands.

principality-of-salm.t: A Vosges principality of the Salm family around the abbey town of Senones, which voted to join France in 1793.
principality-of-salm.o: The counts of Salm, a branch of the Wild- and Rhinegraves, held lands in the Vosges around Senones and Badonviller. In 1623 Philip Otto of Salm was made a prince of the Holy Roman Empire, and the territory became a principality.
principality-of-salm.r: The principality was a small mountain land of forests, ironworks and later textile workshops. Its life centred on Senones and its Benedictine abbey, whose abbot Dom Augustin Calmet was a celebrated scholar. In 1751 the territory was reorganised and Senones became the princes' residence, with a modest court.
principality-of-salm.e: Surrounded by Revolutionary France and cut off by its blockade, the inhabitants voted to join France, and the French First Republic annexed the principality in 1793. The Salm-Salm princes received compensation in Westphalia.

pellendones.t: A Celtiberian people of the upper Douro around the Picos de Urbión, living in the high country north of Numantia.
pellendones.o: The Pellendones lived around the sources of the Douro in northern Soria and southern La Rioja from about the 4th century BCE. Pliny counts them among the Celtiberians, and some ancient geographers placed Numantia in their territory rather than that of the Arevaci.
pellendones.r: They were a highland people of hillforts and herding, with towns such as Visontium and Augustobriga named by Ptolemy. Their society was probably organised in clans under local elites like that of their Celtiberian neighbours, but no details are recorded.
pellendones.e: They were drawn into the Celtiberian wars against Rome and came under Roman control after the fall of Numantia in 133 BCE, becoming part of Hispania Citerior.

principality-of-anhalt-dessau.t: The leading Anhalt principality, famed for the Old Dessauer's drill reforms and the Dessau-Wörlitz Garden Realm of the Enlightenment.
principality-of-anhalt-dessau.o: Anhalt-Dessau was created in the 1603 partition of Anhalt, with Prince John George I receiving Dessau on the Mulde near its junction with the Elbe. The line was Calvinist and closely tied to the Electorate of Brandenburg by marriage.
principality-of-anhalt-dessau.r: Leopold I, the Old Dessauer, was a Prussian field marshal who introduced the iron ramrod and cadenced marching. His grandson Leopold III Friedrich Franz was a model Enlightenment ruler who laid out the landscape gardens of Wörlitz, built schools and founded the Philanthropinum, a progressive school, in 1774. The principality became a duchy in 1807.
principality-of-anhalt-dessau.e: Anhalt-Dessau inherited Anhalt-Köthen in 1847 and Anhalt-Bernburg in 1863, after which Duke Leopold IV Friedrich ruled a united Duchy of Anhalt from Dessau. The Garden Realm is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

principality-of-orange.t: A tiny sovereign principality in the Rhône valley whose title passed to the house of Nassau and gave the Dutch royal family its name.
principality-of-orange.o: Orange was a Roman colony and later a county within the Kingdom of Arles; the troubadour Raimbaut d'Orange ruled part of it in the 12th century. In 1163 Emperor Frederick Barbarossa raised it to a principality, and it passed in 1173 to Bertrand of Baux, whose family ruled it for over two centuries.
principality-of-orange.r: The principality was a small enclave inside Provence and the Comtat Venaissin, with Roman monuments, a university founded in 1365 and its own courts. It passed to the Chalon family in 1393. René of Chalon left it to his cousin William of Nassau in 1544, and under William the Silent Orange became a refuge for Protestants.
principality-of-orange.e: Louis XIV occupied Orange several times and destroyed its fortifications. After the death of William III of England in 1702, France took it, and the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713 recognised its annexation. The princes of Orange-Nassau kept the title, which the Dutch royal house still bears.

principality-of-salerno.t: Lombard principality of southern Italy, home of the famous medical school of Salerno, conquered by Robert Guiscard in 1077.
principality-of-salerno.o: A long civil war in the Principality of Benevento ended in 849 with a formal partition: Siconulf became prince of Salerno, ruling the western half including the coast of Campania, Lucania and parts of Calabria, while Radelchis kept Benevento.
principality-of-salerno.r: Salerno was a prosperous coastal city with links to Amalfi and the Byzantine world. The Schola Medica Salernitana, the first great medical school of medieval Europe, flourished there from the 10th century, drawing on Greek, Latin and Arabic learning. Under Guaimar IV (1027–1052) the principality reached its height, controlling Amalfi, Sorrento and Capua, and he invested the Norman leaders with Apulia.
principality-of-salerno.e: After Guaimar IV was murdered in 1052, Norman power grew rapidly. Robert Guiscard, who had married Sichelgaita, sister of Prince Gisulf II, besieged Salerno and took it in 1077, making it his capital. The principality became part of the Norman Duchy of Apulia.

pellene.t: Easternmost city of Achaea, a loyal Spartan ally famous for the woollen cloaks given as prizes at its games.
pellene.o: Pellene stood on a high hill in eastern Achaea, near the border with Sicyon, a short way inland from the Gulf of Corinth. It was one of the twelve Achaean cities, formed in the early Iron Age.
pellene.r: Pellene was known for its warm woollen cloaks, awarded as prizes at its local games, and for its sanctuary of Athena. Unlike most Achaean cities, it sided with Sparta at the start of the Peloponnesian War. In the 4th century BCE it was ruled at times by tyrants, including the wrestler Chaeron, who was installed with Macedonian backing.
pellene.e: Pellene joined the revived Achaean League. In 241 BCE the Aetolian League sacked it, and Aratus routed the Aetolians in its streets. It passed under Roman control in 146 BCE and later dwindled.

principality-of-capua.t: Lombard principality of northern Campania that broke away from Benevento and later became the first Norman principality in southern Italy.
principality-of-capua.o: In the civil wars of the Lombard south in the 840s, Landulf I, gastald of Capua, made his town practically independent of both Benevento and Salerno. Arab raiders destroyed old Capua in 841, and in 856 his family founded a new Capua on the site of Casilinum by the Volturno. Its rulers took the title of prince by the early 10th century.
principality-of-capua.r: Capua was ruled by quarrelsome branches of Landulf's family, who controlled northern Campania and much of the Liri valley. Pandulf Ironhead (died 981) briefly united Capua, Benevento and Spoleto under imperial patronage. Pandulf IV, called the Wolf of the Abruzzi, despoiled Monte Cassino and hired Norman mercenaries, helping the Normans establish themselves at Aversa.
principality-of-capua.e: The Norman Richard I of Aversa took Capua in 1058, and his family ruled it as princes for nearly eighty years. After Robert II of Capua resisted Roger II, the principality was absorbed into the Kingdom of Sicily in 1135.

phocian-league.t: Federation of the towns of Phocis in central Greece, which seized Delphi and fought the Third Sacred War against Thebes and Philip II.
phocian-league.o: The Phocians lived in the valley of the Cephissus and around Mount Parnassus, in some twenty small towns such as Elateia. By the 6th century BCE they formed a federation with a common council house, the Phokikon. Their long wars with the Thessalians included famous stratagems with chalk-whitened warriors.
phocian-league.r: Phocis guarded the path around Thermopylae and fought in 480 BCE before submitting to Persia. In 356 BCE, fined by the Amphictyony, the Phocians under Philomelus seized Delphi and used its treasure to hire mercenaries. Onomarchus twice defeated Philip II in 353 BCE but was killed at the Battle of the Crocus Field in 352 BCE.
phocian-league.e: In 346 BCE Phalaecus surrendered to Philip II. The Phocian towns were broken into villages, Phocis lost its vote in the Amphictyony and owed annual indemnities to Delphi. It later revived as a league.

prince-bishopric-of-schwerin.t: Small Mecklenburg church state founded during the conversion of the Obotrites and absorbed by the dukes of Mecklenburg after the Reformation.
prince-bishopric-of-schwerin.o: The bishopric was set up by Henry the Lion during the conquest of the Slavic Obotrites, with the Cistercian monk Berno as its first bishop and its seat moved to Schwerin around 1160. After Henry's fall in 1180 the bishops held their estates as imperial princes, a status the dukes of Mecklenburg constantly disputed.
prince-bishopric-of-schwerin.r: The territory was small, consisting chiefly of lands around Bützow, where the bishops resided, and Warin. It grew through German settlement in former Slavic lands. In the 16th century the see was held by princes of the Mecklenburg house, such as Ulrich of Mecklenburg, and became Lutheran, so the bishopric functioned in practice as a Mecklenburg appanage.
prince-bishopric-of-schwerin.e: The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 secularised it as the Principality of Schwerin and awarded it to the Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin as compensation for Wismar, which went to Sweden. It is now part of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

principality-of-nassau-siegen.t: Iron-mining Nassau principality in the Siegerland, divided for a century between Catholic and Protestant branches of the house.
principality-of-nassau-siegen.o: After the death of Count John VI of Nassau-Dillenburg in 1606, his lands were divided and his son John VII received Siegen. Siegen was the birthplace of Peter Paul Rubens in 1577, when his parents lived there in exile.
principality-of-nassau-siegen.r: The Siegerland's iron ore and forges made it relatively prosperous. The house split confessionally: John VIII converted to Catholicism and his line held part of the land while the Reformed line held the rest, so Siegen had two castles, the Upper and Lower. Johan Maurits of Nassau-Siegen, governor of Dutch Brazil, belonged to the Reformed branch. Counts became princes in 1652 and 1664.
principality-of-nassau-siegen.e: The Reformed line died out in 1734 and the Catholic line in 1743, and the territory passed to Prince William IV of Orange-Nassau as part of Nassau-Diez. It later went to the Grand Duchy of Berg and in 1815 to the Kingdom of Prussia.

principality-of-gjirokaster.t: Albanian lordship of the Zenebishi family in southern Albania, one of the last Christian powers in Epirus before the Ottoman conquest.
principality-of-gjirokaster.o: Gjon Zenebishi, an Albanian chieftain whose clan had moved into Epirus during the 14th-century Albanian migrations, took the fortress of Gjirokastër (Argyrokastron) around 1386. He extended his rule over the Drino valley and parts of Chameria, and the Byzantine court recognised him with the title of sebastokrator.
principality-of-gjirokaster.r: The lordship was a clan-based military domain built around the hilltop citadel of Gjirokastër and its villages. Gjon fought the Italian rulers of the Despotate of Epirus at Ioannina, capturing Esau de' Buondelmonti in 1399, and courted Venice, which controlled nearby Corfu. Society rested on Albanian pastoral clans and an Orthodox Greek and Albanian peasantry.
principality-of-gjirokaster.e: Repeated Ottoman campaigns under Sultan Mehmed I wore the lordship down, and Gjirokastër fell in 1418, the year Gjon died. His son Depa fled to Venetian territory and later led a failed rising in 1434. The town became the centre of an Ottoman sanjak.

prince-abbey-of-corvey.t: The leading Carolingian abbey of Saxony, a base for missions to the north and home of the chronicler Widukind, whose westwork is a World Heritage Site.
prince-abbey-of-corvey.o: Corvey was founded in 822 on the Weser near Höxter by monks from Corbie in Picardy, led by Adalard and Wala, cousins of Charlemagne, with the support of Louis the Pious. It was intended to anchor Christianity in newly conquered Saxony, and in 836 it received the relics of Saint Vitus from Saint-Denis.
prince-abbey-of-corvey.r: Corvey sent Ansgar on his mission to Denmark and Sweden, and its school produced Widukind of Corvey, whose Deeds of the Saxons is a chief source for the Ottonian kings. The abbots were princes of the Empire ruling a small territory around Höxter. Its Carolingian westwork, completed in 885, is one of the few surviving from the period.
prince-abbey-of-corvey.e: Corvey shrank after the Thirty Years' War. In 1792 it was raised to a prince-bishopric, but in 1803 it was secularised and given to the Prince of Orange-Nassau-Fulda, then passed to Westphalia and Prussia. The poet Hoffmann von Fallersleben, author of the German national anthem, later worked in its library.

principality-of-arianiti.t: Lands of the Albanian lord Gjergj Arianiti, who led an early revolt against the Ottomans and became Skanderbeg's ally and father-in-law.
principality-of-arianiti.o: The Arianiti were an old noble family of central Albania, holding lands along the Shkumbin valley and around Elbasan. In 1432 Gjergj Arianiti, who had been a hostage at the Ottoman court, led a rising against the new Ottoman land registers and defeated several Ottoman armies in the mountains between 1432 and 1436.
principality-of-arianiti.r: Little is known of how the lands were governed: they were a mountain lordship of fortified villages and clan levies rather than a state with fixed institutions, and no clear capital is recorded. Gjergj built ties through marriage, wedding his daughter Donika to Skanderbeg in 1451, and negotiated with Venice, Naples and the papacy.
principality-of-arianiti.e: Gjergj Arianiti joined the League of Lezhë in 1444, though he later quarrelled with Skanderbeg. He died in 1462, and the family's lands fell to the Ottomans in the following years. His descendants, the Arianiti Comneni, settled in Italy.

principality-of-anhalt-bernburg.t: The senior Anhalt principality, ruled from a castle above the Saale at Bernburg, whose line survived the longest among the 1603 partitions.
principality-of-anhalt-bernburg.o: When the Principality of Anhalt was divided in 1603 among the heirs of Joachim Ernst, Christian I received Bernburg. Christian was a leading Calvinist politician who directed the policy of the Protestant Union and the Elector Palatine before the defeat at the White Mountain in 1620.
principality-of-anhalt-bernburg.r: The state was small and agrarian, with silver and copper mining in its Harz exclave around Ballenstedt and Harzgerode. The ruling line was Calvinist. Branch lines split off, including Anhalt-Bernburg-Schaumburg-Hoym. Bernburg held the seniority among the Anhalt princes and was raised to a duchy in 1806, with the court later moving partly to Ballenstedt.
principality-of-anhalt-bernburg.e: The last duke, Alexander Karl, died childless in 1863, and his lands passed to Anhalt-Dessau, which thus united all the Anhalt territories into the Duchy of Anhalt. Bernburg remained a district town within Anhalt.

perusia.t: Etruscan hill city above the upper Tiber, known for its gates, its family tombs and a famous siege by Octavian in 41–40 BCE.
perusia.o: Perusia, Etruscan Persna, modern Perugia, grew on a group of hills west of the Tiber, near the border with the Umbrians. It developed into a city later than the coastal centres, gaining importance from the 6th century BCE and especially in the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE, when its great walls and gates were built.
perusia.r: Perusia controlled river routes and farmland on the upper Tiber and mixed with Umbrian neighbours. Its aristocratic families buried their dead in chamber tombs with carved urns, the finest being the Hypogeum of the Volumni. The Cippus of Perugia, a stone boundary text of about 150 words, is one of the longest Etruscan inscriptions, and the Arco Etrusco gate still stands.
perusia.e: Perusia joined other Etruscan cities against Rome, made truces in 310 and 294 BCE and became a Roman ally after the wars of the early 3rd century. In the Perusine War Octavian besieged Lucius Antonius there in 41–40 BCE; the city was taken and burned. Augustus rebuilt it as Augusta Perusia.

polyrrhenia.t: Fortified hill city of western Crete, the leading power of the island's far west in the Hellenistic period.
polyrrhenia.o: Polyrrhenia stood on a steep hill south of the Gulf of Kissamos in western Crete. Strabo says it was founded by Achaeans and Laconians, who united the scattered villages of the area. Its name, meaning rich in flocks, reflects its pastoral economy.
polyrrhenia.r: Polyrrhenia controlled the west of Crete, with harbours at Phalasarna and Kisamos at times under its influence. It had kosmoi magistrates like other Cretan cities. In the Lyttian War of 220 BCE it broke with Knossos and allied with Philip V of the Antigonid Kingdom of Macedonia. Its walls and cisterns survive.
polyrrhenia.e: Polyrrhenia came under Roman rule in the conquest of Crete in 69 to 67 BCE and continued as a town, later a Byzantine bishopric.

parisii.t: Gallic people of the middle Seine whose town Lutetia became Paris.
parisii.o: The Parisii settled on the Seine in the 3rd century BCE and controlled river traffic across the Paris basin. Caesar mentions that he held a council of Gaul at Lutetia in 53 BCE. The exact site of their oppidum is debated; excavations at Nanterre have revealed a large Gallic settlement.
parisii.r: They struck fine gold coins, among the most elegant in Gaul. Their wealth came from trade on the Seine, and Roman inscriptions later record a powerful guild of boatmen.
parisii.e: In 52 BCE they joined the revolt; the Aulercan leader Camulogenus burned Lutetia and was defeated by Caesar's legate Labienus. Under Rome Lutetia was rebuilt on the Montagne Sainte-Geneviève, where the boatmen dedicated the Pillar of the Boatmen to Jupiter. In late antiquity the town took the name of the people, Paris.

prince-bishopric-of-verdun.t: One of the Three Bishoprics of Lorraine, a church principality on the Meuse that passed from the Empire to France between 1552 and 1648.
prince-bishopric-of-verdun.o: Verdun, where the Carolingian empire was divided in 843, was an ancient bishopric. In 997 Emperor Otto III granted Bishop Haimo the comital rights over the city and its district, making the bishops princes of the Holy Roman Empire.
prince-bishopric-of-verdun.r: The bishops' temporal lands were small and lay along the Meuse, and they faced constant pressure from the counts of Bar and the dukes of Lorraine. The citizens of Verdun gained wide self-government and imperial-city status, limiting the bishops' power at home. The city was a trading centre, known for its sugared almonds.
prince-bishopric-of-verdun.e: Henry II of France occupied Verdun with Metz and Toul in 1552, and the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 confirmed French sovereignty over the Three Bishoprics. Verdun became part of the Kingdom of France and later a major fortress.

papal-states.t: The territories of central Italy ruled by the popes as temporal sovereigns for over a thousand years, from Pepin's donation to the capture of Rome in 1870.
papal-states.o: When the Lombards threatened Rome, Pope Stephen II won the protection of the Frankish king Pepin the Short in 754. Pepin defeated the Lombards and in 756 gave the pope the lands of the former Exarchate of Ravenna together with the Duchy of Rome. Charlemagne confirmed and extended the grant in 774.
papal-states.r: The pope ruled as an elected monarch through cardinals, legates and governors, but for centuries real control was weak, contested by Roman nobles and local lords. Innocent III expanded papal power, and Cardinal Albornoz reasserted it in the 1350s with the Egidian Constitutions. Renaissance popes such as Alexander VI and Julius II fought to bring the Romagna under control and built the new St Peter's. Ferrara (1598) and Urbino (1631) were later absorbed.
papal-states.e: Napoleon annexed the States in 1809; they were restored in 1815. In 1860 Romagna, the Marche and Umbria joined the Kingdom of Italy, and on 20 September 1870 Italian troops entered Rome. Pius IX refused to recognise the loss, and the dispute was settled by the Lateran Treaty of 1929, creating Vatican City.

palace-state-of-zakros.t: The easternmost Minoan palace on Crete, a harbour centre for trade with Egypt and the Levant, found unplundered with its treasures in place.
palace-state-of-zakros.o: Zakros lies in a sheltered bay at the eastern tip of Crete, a natural harbour facing Egypt, Cyprus and the Levant. A settlement existed in the Early Minoan period, and a palace was built c. 1900 BCE. The surviving palace, smaller than Knossos or Phaistos, dates mostly from the Neopalatial period after c. 1700 BCE.
palace-state-of-zakros.r: The palace followed the standard Minoan plan with a central court, storerooms, workshops, a lustral basin and a cistern room. It likely controlled trade in copper, ivory and elephant tusks, some of which were found on site. Its treasury held stone ritual vessels, including a rock-crystal rhyton, and Linear A tablets show local record-keeping.
palace-state-of-zakros.e: Zakros was destroyed by fire c. 1450 BCE and abandoned so suddenly that it was never looted. It was not reoccupied as a palace. Nikolaos Platon excavated it from 1961, recovering one of the richest collections of Minoan objects found in place.

principality-of-lucca-and-piombino.t: The Tuscan principality Napoleon created for his sister Elisa Bonaparte, who governed it as an energetic reforming ruler.
principality-of-lucca-and-piombino.o: In 1805 Napoleon abolished the Republic of Lucca and joined it to the Principality of Piombino, granting the new state to his sister Elisa and her husband Felice Baciocchi. Massa and Carrara were added in 1806.
principality-of-lucca-and-piombino.r: Elisa, not her husband, held real power. She introduced the Napoleonic Code, closed many convents, reorganised schools and finances, and promoted the Carrara marble industry, founding an academy and workshops that produced busts of the Bonaparte family for all Europe. She patronised the violinist Niccolò Paganini at her court. In 1809 Napoleon also made her Grand Duchess of Tuscany, ruling from Florence.
principality-of-lucca-and-piombino.e: Elisa fled as Napoleon's empire collapsed in 1814. The Congress of Vienna gave Lucca to Maria Luisa of Bourbon as the Duchy of Lucca, while Piombino went to the Grand Duchy of Tuscany.

provisional-government-of-national-defen.t: Rival Greek government set up in Thessaloniki in 1916 by Eleftherios Venizelos, which took Greece into the First World War on the Allied side.
provisional-government-of-national-defen.o: During the First World War, King Constantine I insisted on neutrality while Prime Minister Eleftherios Venizelos wanted to join the Entente. After Venizelos was forced out, officers in Allied-held Thessaloniki launched the National Defence movement in August 1916. In September and October Venizelos formed a provisional government there with Admiral Pavlos Kountouriotis and General Panagiotis Danglis.
provisional-government-of-national-defen.r: The government, led by this triumvirate, controlled northern Greece, Crete and most of the Aegean islands with Allied support, raised an army and declared war on Bulgaria and Germany. Greece was split in two, the National Schism, while Allied pressure on Athens led to the armed clash of December 1916, the Noemvriana.
provisional-government-of-national-defen.e: In June 1917 the Allies forced Constantine I to leave the country. Venizelos returned to Athens as prime minister of a united Kingdom of Greece, which entered the war fully. The bitterness of the schism shaped Greek politics for decades.

prince-bishopric-of-cambrai.t: An imperial church principality on the French border, which gave its name to the League of Cambrai and the Ladies' Peace before Louis XIV annexed it.
prince-bishopric-of-cambrai.o: Cambrai was a Merovingian bishopric whose diocese stretched across Hainaut and Brabant. In 1007 Emperor Henry II granted the county of Cambrai to Bishop Erluin, making the bishops princes of the Holy Roman Empire on its frontier with France.
prince-bishopric-of-cambrai.r: The Cambrésis was a small but rich land of cloth and linen, its name later given to the fine fabric cambric. The bishops often struggled with the townspeople and with the counts of Flanders and Hainaut. The city hosted the League of Cambrai against Venice in 1508 and the Ladies' Peace of 1529. Charles V built a citadel there in 1543.
prince-bishopric-of-cambrai.e: Cambrai became an archbishopric in 1559 under strong Spanish influence. Louis XIV captured it in 1677, and the Treaty of Nijmegen of 1678 gave it to the Kingdom of France. Fénelon was its most famous archbishop.

principality-of-anhalt-zerbst.t: Small Anhalt principality on the Elbe best remembered as the birthplace dynasty of Catherine the Great of Russia.
principality-of-anhalt-zerbst.o: Rudolf, a son of Joachim Ernst, received Zerbst in the 1603 partition of Anhalt. The town, north of the Elbe, had been a prosperous brewing centre known for its beer, and the line included the lordship of Jever in Frisia, inherited in 1667.
principality-of-anhalt-zerbst.r: The principality was Lutheran in its later period and modestly governed from a baroque palace in Zerbst. Its most famous member was Sophie Auguste Friederike, daughter of Prince Christian August, who married the future Peter III and became Empress Catherine II of Russia. Her brother Friedrich August, the last prince, lived mostly abroad and hired out soldiers to Britain during the American Revolutionary War.
principality-of-anhalt-zerbst.e: Friedrich August died without heirs in 1793. The principality was divided among the other Anhalt lines, Dessau, Bernburg and Köthen, while Jever passed to Catherine the Great and so to Russia.

panormus.t: Phoenician and Punic city on the bay of Palermo, Carthage's chief stronghold in western Sicily until Rome captured it in 254 BCE.
panormus.o: Phoenicians settled Panormus, called Ziz ('flower') on its coins, on a promontory between two river inlets by the late 8th or 7th century BCE. Its deep natural harbour gave it the Greek name Panormos, 'all-harbour'. With Motya and Soloeis it formed the cluster of Phoenician towns in western Sicily that came under Carthaginian protection.
panormus.r: Panormus prospered from trade between Carthage, Sardinia and the Greek and Elymian towns of Sicily and served as a key Carthaginian military base: Hamilcar landed there before the battle of Himera in 480 BCE. Its necropolis shows a mixed population of Phoenicians, Greeks and Elymians. It minted coins with Punic and Greek legends and was ruled by local magistrates under Carthaginian oversight.
panormus.e: In the First Punic War Rome took Panormus in 254 BCE, and in 250 BCE the consul Lucius Caecilius Metellus defeated a Carthaginian army with elephants beneath its walls. The city became a free town of the Roman province of Sicily and later grew into Palermo, capital of the Emirate of Sicily and the Norman kingdom.

principality-of-correggio.t: The small Emilian state of the da Correggio lords, birthplace of the painter Antonio Allegri, called Correggio.
principality-of-correggio.o: The da Correggio family had ruled the town of Correggio, between Reggio and Carpi, since the 12th century and had been powerful in Parma. In 1452 Emperor Frederick III recognised their lands as a county, raised to a principality in 1616.
principality-of-correggio.r: The counts governed a small farming territory and a fortified town with a lively court. Veronica Gambara, poet and widow of Count Giberto, ruled as regent in the early 16th century and corresponded with leading writers. The painter Antonio Allegri, known as Correggio, was born in the town around 1489. The rulers depended on the protection of the emperor and their Este neighbours.
principality-of-correggio.e: Prince Siro da Correggio was accused of minting debased coins and was deposed by the emperor in 1630. In 1635 the principality was sold to Francesco I d'Este and joined to the Duchy of Modena and Reggio.

peucetians.t: Iapygian people of central Apulia around modern Bari, whose towns such as Rubi became centres of Greek-influenced art and vase collecting.
peucetians.o: The Peucetians occupied central Apulia between the Daunians to the north and the Messapians to the south, from the early 1st millennium BCE. Greek writers explained their name through Peucetius, a son of the Arcadian Lycaon, but their culture developed from local Iron Age communities related to their Iapygian neighbours.
peucetians.r: They lived in separate fortified towns, among them Caelia, Azetium, Rubi (Ruvo di Puglia) and the site of Monte Sannace, without a known central government. Their geometric painted pottery gave way, from the 5th century BCE, to strong Greek influence: the elite of Rubi buried their dead with Athenian and Apulian red-figure vases, many from Taras. They grew cereals and olives and traded through coastal landings.
peucetians.e: The Peucetian towns came under Roman control around the end of the 4th and start of the 3rd centuries BCE during Rome's expansion into Apulia. They were later absorbed into Roman Apulia and became municipia. Collections of vases from Ruvo, such as the Jatta collection, preserve much of their material culture.

principality-of-pontecorvo.t: A tiny papal enclave in southern Lazio that Napoleon granted to Marshal Bernadotte, the future king of Sweden.
principality-of-pontecorvo.o: Pontecorvo, a small town on the Liri river surrounded by the Kingdom of Naples, belonged to the Papal States. In 1806 Napoleon seized it and made Marshal Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte its sovereign prince.
principality-of-pontecorvo.r: Bernadotte never visited and ruled through local administrators who applied French laws. In 1810 he was elected crown prince of Sweden and gave up the principality, which Napoleon in 1812 granted to Lucien Murat, son of King Joachim Murat of the Kingdom of Naples (1806–1815).
principality-of-pontecorvo.e: After Napoleon's fall, the Congress of Vienna returned Pontecorvo to the Papal States in 1815. Bernadotte became King Charles XIV John of Sweden in 1818.

parisii-britain.t: East Yorkshire people known for the Arras culture of square-barrow and chariot burials, sharing their name with the Parisii of Gaul.
parisii-britain.o: The Parisii are identified with the Arras culture of the Yorkshire Wolds, which from about the 4th century BCE buried its dead under small square barrows, sometimes with dismantled two-wheeled vehicles, as at Wetwang and Garton Slack. The likeness of these burials to rites in northern Gaul, and the shared name with the Parisii of the Seine, has fuelled long debate over migration or contact.
parisii-britain.r: Society was based on mixed farming on the chalk Wolds and in the Vale of Pickering, with large cemeteries of thousands of barrows. Chariot burials of men and women, with harness fittings, mirrors and brooches, point to an elite who displayed status through horses and fine metalwork. No coinage is attributed to them and no rulers are named.
parisii-britain.e: The area came under Roman control during the campaigns of Petillius Cerialis against the Brigantes from 71. Ptolemy later listed Petuaria as their town, and an inscription from Brough-on-Humber records the civitas of the Parisi, which administered the region under Roman Britain.

prince-bishopric-of-metz.t: The largest of the Three Bishoprics of Lorraine, an ecclesiastical principality of the Empire ruled from Vic-sur-Seille after Metz itself broke free.
prince-bishopric-of-metz.o: Metz had been a bishopric since Roman times and a Carolingian centre of liturgy and chant. In the late 10th century the Ottonian kings confirmed the bishops' secular lordship over the city and scattered lands in Lorraine, making them princes of the Holy Roman Empire.
prince-bishopric-of-metz.r: The bishops' territory was fragmented and lay largely around the Seille valley, with salt works at Vic and Marsal providing revenue. By the 13th century the citizens of Metz had won independence as the Free Imperial City of Metz, so the bishops ruled from Vic-sur-Seille. They often struggled with the dukes of Lorraine.
prince-bishopric-of-metz.e: In 1552 Henry II of France seized Metz, Toul and Verdun, and the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 confirmed French sovereignty over the Three Bishoprics. The bishopric then became part of the Kingdom of France.

prince-bishopric-of-strasbourg.t: The Alsatian church principality whose bishops lost their cathedral city to its burghers in 1262 but kept a territory on both banks of the Rhine until 1803.
prince-bishopric-of-strasbourg.o: Strasbourg had been a bishopric since late Roman times. In 982 Emperor Otto II granted the bishop extensive rights over the city, and later Ottonian and Salian grants added counties and estates in Alsace and the Ortenau, making the bishops princes of the Holy Roman Empire.
prince-bishopric-of-strasbourg.r: The bishops began the great Romanesque cathedral under Bishop Werner in 1015. In 1262 the citizens defeated Bishop Walter of Geroldseck at Hausbergen and the city became the Free Imperial City of Strasbourg, so the bishops governed from Saverne. Their lands lay in scattered pieces across lower Alsace and the right bank of the Rhine.
prince-bishopric-of-strasbourg.e: After Louis XIV took Strasbourg in 1681 the left-bank lands came under French sovereignty, and a line of Rohan cardinals held the see. The Revolution abolished the bishops' rights in Alsace, and the right-bank remainder was secularised and given to Baden in 1803.

phlius.t: Small inland city of the north-eastern Peloponnese, renowned for its steadfast loyalty to Sparta and its long siege by Agesilaus.
phlius.o: Phlius occupied an upland valley south-west of Corinth, at the head of the Asopus river. Dorian settlers from Argos formed the city in the early Iron Age. It was a small agricultural state known for its wine.
phlius.r: Phlius was usually an oligarchy and a loyal member of the Peloponnesian League. A democratic faction took power in the 380s BCE, and Agesilaus II of Sparta besieged the city from 381 to 379 BCE to restore the exiles. Xenophon praised the Phliasians for their faithfulness to Sparta during Theban invasions in the 360s BCE. The dramatist Pratinas, credited with the satyr play, was a citizen.
phlius.e: Phlius joined the Achaean League in 229 BCE, after its tyrant stepped down, and passed under Roman control in 146 BCE.

poseidonia.t: Greek colony on the Gulf of Salerno, later called Paestum, with three of the best-preserved Doric temples anywhere.
poseidonia.o: Colonists from Sybaris founded Poseidonia around 600 BCE on the plain near the mouth of the Sele river, giving Sybaris an outlet on the Tyrrhenian Sea. Named after Poseidon, the city was laid out on a grid and enclosed later by walls nearly 5 km long.
poseidonia.r: Poseidonia prospered from farming and trade with the Etruscans and native peoples. Its three Doric temples, the so-called Basilica of about 550 BCE, the Temple of Athena and the temple of about 460 BCE once called the Temple of Neptune, still stand. The sanctuary of Hera at the mouth of the Sele and the painted Tomb of the Diver of about 470 BCE are famous.
poseidonia.e: Around 410 BCE the Lucanians took over the city, which became Paistom, and Greek and Lucanian customs blended. In 273 BCE Rome founded the Latin colony of Paestum there. Malaria and silting led to its abandonment in the Middle Ages, which helped preserve the temples.

principality-of-bidache.t: A tiny sovereign lordship on the edge of the Basque Country whose Gramont lords claimed independence from France until the Revolution.
principality-of-bidache.o: Bidache, on the Bidouze river between Béarn, Navarre and the Labourd, belonged to the Gramont family. Exploiting its uncertain position on the frontier of Navarre and France, the Gramonts asserted full sovereignty over it, and the register dates the principality from 1570.
principality-of-bidache.r: The Gramonts ruled the small territory from their castle at Bidache, administering justice and taxation without royal interference, while serving the French kings at court and in war. Antoine III de Gramont was a marshal of France and diplomat under Louis XIV. The lands were rural, with Gascon and Basque speakers.
principality-of-bidache.e: The Revolution abolished the Gramonts' privileges, and in 1790 Bidache was incorporated into France and the new department of Basses-Pyrénées. The ruined castle remains.

principality-of-wales-under-owain-glyndw.t: The last attempt at an independent Welsh state, led by Owain Glyndwr, who was proclaimed Prince of Wales in 1400 and held parliaments at Machynlleth.
principality-of-wales-under-owain-glyndw.o: Owain Glyndwr, a descendant of the princes of Powys Fadog and Deheubarth, was proclaimed Prince of Wales by his followers in September 1400 after a land dispute with Lord Grey of Ruthin. His revolt quickly spread across Wales, fed by anger at English rule and taxes.
principality-of-wales-under-owain-glyndw.r: By 1404 Glyndwr held most of Wales, took Harlech and Aberystwyth castles, and summoned parliaments at Machynlleth and Harlech. He allied with France and with English rebels, the Percys and Mortimers, and in the Pennal Letter proposed an independent Welsh church and two universities.
principality-of-wales-under-owain-glyndw.e: From 1405 English forces under Prince Henry recovered ground, retaking Aberystwyth and Harlech by 1409. Glyndwr vanished around 1415. He became a lasting symbol of Welsh national identity.

palace-state-of-malia.t: Minoan palace centre on Crete's north coast, one of the island's great Bronze Age palaces and the source of the famous gold bee pendant.
palace-state-of-malia.o: Malia grew from an Early Minoan settlement on a fertile coastal plain east of Knossos. Around 1950 BCE, in the Protopalatial period, a monumental palace was built around a central court, making it one of the earliest palace centres on Crete alongside Knossos and Phaistos. The palace was destroyed c. 1700 BCE, probably by earthquake, and rebuilt on a similar plan.
palace-state-of-malia.r: Its rulers are unknown, as Minoan scripts remain undeciphered, but the palace stored grain, oil and wine in large pithoi and organised craft production. The nearby Quartier Mu workshops produced seals, pottery and metalwork, and the Chrysolakkos burial complex yielded the gold pendant of two bees. Inscriptions in Cretan hieroglyphic and Linear A show an administrative system shared with other palaces.
palace-state-of-malia.e: Like most Cretan palaces, Malia was destroyed by fire c. 1450 BCE, in the wave of destructions that preceded Mycenaean dominance from Knossos. It was not rebuilt as a palace, though limited settlement continued. Excavated by French archaeologists since 1915, it is among the best-preserved Minoan sites.

pale-of-calais.t: England's last foothold in mainland France, a fortified port and wool staple held for two centuries after Edward III's siege of 1346–1347.
pale-of-calais.o: After his victory at Crécy, Edward III besieged Calais for eleven months and took it in 1347; the story of the six burghers who offered their lives is famous. The English expelled much of the population and settled the town with English colonists, adding a surrounding district of marsh and forts, the Pale.
pale-of-calais.r: Calais was garrisoned by the largest standing force of the English crown. From 1363 it hosted the Staple, through which England's raw wool exports passed, and the Merchants of the Staple funded its defence. From 1536 it sent members to the English Parliament. It was a base for English armies in France for two centuries.
pale-of-calais.e: In January 1558, during a war in alliance with Spain, Francis, duke of Guise, captured Calais in a surprise winter attack. Mary I reportedly said that Calais would be found written on her heart. The Pale became part of the Kingdom of France.

peloponnesian-senate.t: Revolutionary governing body of the Peloponnese in the first year of the Greek War of Independence, dominated by the region's notables.
peloponnesian-senate.o: When the Greek revolt broke out in March 1821, Petros Mavromichalis formed the Messenian Senate at Kalamata. In May and June 1821 leading notables and clergy of the Peloponnese met at the monastery of Kaltezes and created the Peloponnesian Senate to direct the war and administer liberated territory, later based at Tripolitsa after its capture.
peloponnesian-senate.r: The senate was controlled by the Peloponnesian primates (kodjabashis), local landowners and tax-farmers who had held power under the Ottomans, with Petrobey Mavromichalis as president. It organised supplies and taxes for the siege of Tripolitsa and quarrelled with Demetrios Ypsilantis, who claimed national leadership, and with military chiefs such as Theodoros Kolokotronis.
peloponnesian-senate.e: The First National Assembly at Epidaurus in January 1822 created a central Provisional Administration, the First Hellenic Republic. The regional senate was subordinated and soon dissolved, though the rivalry between notables and military leaders continued into the civil wars of 1823-1825.

principality-of-stavelot-malmedy.t: Tiny ecclesiastical principality of the Ardennes, ruled for over a thousand years by the abbots of twin monasteries.
principality-of-stavelot-malmedy.o: Around 648 to 651 the missionary Remaclus founded twin abbeys at Stavelot and Malmedy in the Ardennes forest, on land granted by Sigebert III of Austrasia. The two houses shared a single abbot, and the community became one of the leading monasteries of the region.
principality-of-stavelot-malmedy.r: In the Holy Roman Empire the abbots became princes with a seat in the Imperial Diet, ruling a small territory between the Prince-Bishopric of Liège and the Duchy of Luxembourg. Abbot Wibald in the 12th century was an adviser to emperors, and the abbey's workshops produced masterpieces of Mosan goldsmith work such as the Stavelot Triptych.
principality-of-stavelot-malmedy.e: Revolutionary France annexed the principality in 1795 and dissolved the abbeys. In 1815 Stavelot went to the Netherlands, and later Belgium, while Malmedy passed to Prussia. Malmedy was transferred to Belgium in 1920, reuniting the two towns.

patrae.t: Achaean city at the mouth of the Gulf of Corinth, a founder of the Achaean League and forerunner of modern Patras.
patrae.o: Patrae was formed, according to Pausanias, by uniting the villages of Aroe, Antheia and Mesatis on the coast of western Achaea. It was one of the twelve Achaean cities and controlled the narrows at the entrance to the Gulf of Corinth.
patrae.r: Patrae was a modest farming and trading town in the Classical period. In 280 BCE it joined Dyme, Tritaea and Pharae in reviving the Achaean League. In 279 BCE the Patraeans were the only Achaeans to send troops against the invading Gauls, suffering heavy losses. The city had a sanctuary of Artemis Laphria.
patrae.e: Patrae passed under Rome in 146 BCE. Augustus made it a Roman colony c. 14 BCE, and it became the chief port of the region, growing into the modern city of Patras.
patrae.re: Greek religion; cult of Artemis Laphria

prince-bishopric-of-havelberg.t: A bishopric founded by Otto I among the Slavs of the Havel, lost in the revolt of 983 and refounded as a small territory that Brandenburg absorbed.
prince-bishopric-of-havelberg.o: Otto I founded the bishopric of Havelberg in 946 or 948 at a stronghold on the Havel, to convert the Slavs of the Northern March. It became a suffragan of the Archbishopric of Magdeburg in 968. The Great Slav Rising of 983 destroyed it, and its bishops lived in exile for more than a century.
prince-bishopric-of-havelberg.r: After the Wendish Crusade of 1147, Bishop Anselm of Havelberg, a noted theologian and diplomat to Byzantium, restored the see, and the cathedral was consecrated in 1170. The bishops ruled a small territory around Havelberg and Wittstock, where they built their residence, but depended on the margraves of Brandenburg.
prince-bishopric-of-havelberg.e: With the Reformation in Brandenburg, the last Catholic bishop died in 1548, and the Hohenzollern electors installed their own family as administrators. The territory was absorbed into the Margraviate of Brandenburg by 1598. The cathedral on the hill at Havelberg survives.

picentes.t: Italic people of the central Adriatic coast, said to have followed a woodpecker to their new land, whose warrior culture lasted until Rome conquered them in 268 BCE.
picentes.o: The Picentes lived in Picenum, the coastal strip and hills of the modern Marche and northern Abruzzo, from the early 1st millennium BCE. Roman tradition said they descended from Sabines who left home in a 'sacred spring' migration, guided by a woodpecker (picus), the bird of Mars. Archaeologists call their culture the Picene culture.
picentes.r: Picene society was dominated by warrior elites buried with helmets, weapons, chariots and amber from the Baltic. Their South Picene inscriptions, in a Sabellic language written in a distinctive alphabet, appear on stone stelae, and the Novilara stele in the north bears a still undeciphered text. Asculum was their main centre, and they traded across the Adriatic and with Etruria.
picentes.e: The Picentes allied with Rome in 299 BCE but revolted in 269 BCE and were conquered in 268 BCE; part of the population was moved to the Gulf of Salerno. Asculum became an allied city, and its massacre of Romans in 91 BCE began the Social War. Picenum became part of Augustus's Regio V.
