principality-of-nassau-hadamar.t: Small Nassau principality in the Westerwald that became a Catholic outpost of the house and left a baroque residence town.
principality-of-nassau-hadamar.o: Hadamar was created in the 1607 division of the lands of John VI of Nassau-Dillenburg and went to his son John Louis. John Louis converted to Catholicism in 1629 and served the emperor as a diplomat at the Peace of Westphalia, for which he was made a prince of the Empire in 1650.
principality-of-nassau-hadamar.r: After its ruler's conversion Hadamar became a Catholic enclave among Protestant Nassau lands, with a Jesuit college and Franciscan friars. John Louis rebuilt Hadamar as a planned residence town with a new palace. The economy was agrarian, with small-scale iron and wool working in the Westerwald hills.
principality-of-nassau-hadamar.e: The line died out with Prince Francis Alexander in 1711, and the territory was divided among the other Nassau-Ottonian lines, Nassau-Diez, Nassau-Siegen and Nassau-Dillenburg. Its lands later passed to the Duchy of Nassau and, in 1866, to Prussia.

powys-fadog.t: The northern half of the Welsh kingdom of Powys, ruled by Madog ap Maredudd's descendants from Castell Dinas Bran above Llangollen.
powys-fadog.o: When Madog ap Maredudd, the last king of all Powys, died in 1160, his kingdom split. The northern part passed to his grandson Madog ap Gruffydd Maelor, after whom it was named Powys Fadog, covering Maelor, Ial, Edeirnion and Cynllaith.
powys-fadog.r: Its princes usually aligned with Gwynedd's Principality of Wales against the English crown. Madog ap Gruffydd founded the Cistercian abbey of Valle Crucis around 1201, and Gruffydd ap Madog built Castell Dinas Bran around 1260.
powys-fadog.e: Powys Fadog's princes backed Llywelyn ap Gruffudd in his final war, and after his death in 1282 Edward I granted the lands to English lords. Its line survived as minor gentry; Owain Glyndwr, who led the Principality of Wales under Owain Glyndwr, descended from it.

principality-of-rugen.t: Slavic principality on the Baltic island of Rügen whose princes, once pagan Rani, became Danish vassals and founders of Stralsund before dying out in 1325.
principality-of-rugen.o: The Slavic Rani ruled Rügen from the temple fortress of Arkona, sanctuary of the god Svantevit. In 1168 King Valdemar I of Denmark and Bishop Absalon stormed Arkona, destroyed the idol and forced the Rani to accept Christianity and Danish overlordship. The native princely house kept its rule as Danish vassals, with Jaromar I as its first Christian prince.
principality-of-rugen.r: The princes held the island and a strip of the Pomeranian mainland, where Wizlaw I granted Stralsund town rights in 1234. They founded monasteries such as Bergen and Eldena and invited German settlers, so Low German gradually replaced the Slavic speech of the Rani. The court combined Danish loyalty with growing ties to the German north, and Wizlaw III composed love songs as a minnesinger.
principality-of-rugen.e: Wizlaw III died without a son in 1325, and the principality passed by inheritance treaty to the Duchy of Pomerania-Wolgast after a war of succession against Mecklenburg. Rügen stayed Pomeranian, then Swedish and Prussian, and is now part of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

pictones.t: Gallic people of Poitou who built ships for Caesar against the Veneti and gave their name to Poitiers and Poitou.
pictones.o: The Pictones held the land south of the lower Loire, around Lemonum (Poitiers), with a coastline on the Atlantic. They were among the larger peoples of western Gaul.
pictones.r: Caesar used their shipyards in 56 BCE for the fleet that defeated the Veneti. Their leader Duratius remained loyal to Rome, which split the people during the revolts.
pictones.e: In 51 BCE Duratius was besieged in Lemonum by Dumnacus of the Andecavi until Roman forces relieved him. Under Rome Lemonum, later called Pictavi, became Poitiers, a major city and bishopric, and the region kept the name Poitou.

principality-of-arches-charleville.t: A sovereign principality on the Meuse where Charles of Gonzaga founded the planned city of Charleville in 1606.
principality-of-arches-charleville.o: Charles of Gonzaga, duke of Nevers and Rethel, held the land of Arches on the Meuse, which claimed to lie outside both France and the Empire. In 1606 he founded a new town there, Charleville, named after himself, and ruled it as a sovereign principality.
principality-of-arches-charleville.r: Charleville was laid out on a regular plan around the Place Ducale, modelled on the Place des Vosges in Paris. The principality minted its own coins and attracted craftsmen with tax exemptions. Charles later became duke of Mantua in 1627, and his Gonzaga heirs ruled the principality from Italy.
principality-of-arches-charleville.e: The last Gonzaga duke, Ferdinando Carlo, died in 1708 after siding with France in the War of the Spanish Succession. Louis XIV then took the principality into the Kingdom of France, though the Condé family claimed it.

prince-bishopric-of-brandenburg.t: An Ottonian missionary bishopric on the Havel that, after a long exile, became a small church territory absorbed by the Hohenzollern electors.
prince-bishopric-of-brandenburg.o: Otto I founded the bishopric of Brandenburg in 948 at the captured Hevelli stronghold of Brenna, as part of his eastern mission, placing it under Magdeburg in 968. In the Great Slav Rising of 983 the Slavs destroyed the see, and its bishops lived as titular exiles until the 12th century.
prince-bishopric-of-brandenburg.r: After Albert the Bear took Brandenburg in 1157, the Premonstratensian cathedral chapter was re-established, and the cathedral on the island in Brandenburg an der Havel was begun in 1165. The bishops held a small territory around Ziesar, where they built their residence, but the margraves dominated them and claimed the right to nominate bishops.
prince-bishopric-of-brandenburg.e: Brandenburg became Lutheran under Elector Joachim II from 1539, and the last Catholic bishop, Matthias von Jagow, accepted the change. The prince-bishopric was secularised and fully incorporated into the Margraviate of Brandenburg by 1571. The cathedral chapter continued as a Protestant institution.

principality-of-piombino.t: A small Tuscan coastal state with the iron mines of Elba, ruled by the Appiani and later the Ludovisi and Boncompagni.
principality-of-piombino.o: In 1399 Gherardo Appiani, lord of Pisa, sold the city to Gian Galeazzo Visconti but kept Piombino, Elba and nearby islands as his own lordship. His family ruled it as lords and, from 1594, as imperial princes.
principality-of-piombino.r: Piombino controlled the iron mines of Elba and the channel between Elba and the mainland, a strategic route for Mediterranean shipping. Its small size made it dependent on stronger powers: Cosimo I de' Medici built Portoferraio on Elba in 1548, and Spain later held Porto Longone. After the Appiani died out, the principality passed to the Ludovisi in 1634 and then to the Boncompagni-Ludovisi.
principality-of-piombino.e: In 1805 Napoleon gave Piombino to his sister Elisa, merging it into the Principality of Lucca and Piombino. In 1815 the Congress of Vienna gave it to the Grand Duchy of Tuscany.

potidaea.t: Corinthian colony on the isthmus of Pallene in Chalcidice whose revolt against Athens in 432 BCE helped trigger the Peloponnesian War.
potidaea.o: Potidaea was founded around 600 BCE by Corinth under the tyrant Periander, whose son Evagoras is named as founder. It stood on the narrow neck of the Pallene peninsula, controlling the way into it, and remained unusually close to its mother city, which still sent it annual magistrates in the 5th century BCE.
potidaea.r: A walled port city with an assembly and magistrates, Potidaea lived from trade in the northern Aegean, Macedonian timber and the produce of Pallene. It held out against the Persian commander Artabazus in 480-479 BCE and fought at Plataea. As a tribute-paying member of the Delian League it was caught between loyalty to Athens and its Corinthian ties.
potidaea.e: Ordered by Athens to pull down its walls and expel the Corinthian magistrates, Potidaea revolted in 432 BCE and surrendered after a costly siege in 430 BCE; Athenian settlers replaced its people. It later joined the Chalcidian League, was retaken by Athens in 364 BCE and was captured by Philip II in 356 BCE. Cassander refounded it as Cassandreia.

prince-bishopric-of-augsburg.t: Swabian church state of the bishops of Augsburg, who were forced out of their own cathedral city and governed instead from Dillingen on the Danube.
prince-bishopric-of-augsburg.o: The diocese of Augsburg dates from late Roman times and was led in the 10th century by Saint Ulrich, who defended the city at the Lechfeld in 955. From the late 12th century the bishops assembled a secular territory along the Lech and Danube. As the city itself won independence as the Free Imperial City of Augsburg, they moved their residence to Dillingen.
prince-bishopric-of-augsburg.r: The cathedral chapter elected the prince-bishop, who ruled scattered lands including Dillingen, Füssen and parts of the Allgäu. Cardinal Otto Truchsess von Waldburg founded the University of Dillingen in 1551, run by the Jesuits from 1563, which made the territory a Counter-Reformation stronghold. Its estates were rural, with farms, forests and small market towns.
prince-bishopric-of-augsburg.e: The territory was secularised in 1802 and annexed by the Electorate of Bavaria, ending the bishops' secular rule; the last prince-bishop, Clemens Wenceslaus of Saxony, was also Elector of Trier. The Catholic diocese of Augsburg continues today.

principality-of-thessaly.t: Greek principality in Thessaly ruled by an offshoot of the Epirote dynasty, independent of Byzantium until the Catalans and Byzantines divided it.
principality-of-thessaly.o: On the death of Michael II of the Despotate of Epirus around 1268, his illegitimate son John I Doukas received Thessaly, with its capital at Neopatras. Byzantine writers called the region Great Vlachia, after its many Vlach inhabitants. John resisted Michael VIII Palaiologos, defeating a Byzantine army at Neopatras around 1275.
principality-of-thessaly.r: John I held the Byzantine title of sebastokrator and ruled a mixed Greek and Vlach population of farmers and herders through local magnates. He allied with the Latin Duchy of Athens and the Principality of Achaea against the restored Byzantine Empire. His sons Constantine and John II continued his policies, John II marrying a daughter of Andronikos II.
principality-of-thessaly.e: When John II died without heirs in 1318, Thessaly broke apart. The Catalan Company, ruling the Duchy of Athens, seized the south and created the Duchy of Neopatras, while local lords and the Byzantines took the north.

principality-of-taranto.t: A great southern Italian fief created for the crusader Bohemond, later held by princes so powerful they rivalled the kings of Naples.
principality-of-taranto.o: After Robert Guiscard's death the Norman inheritance was divided, and in 1088 his eldest son Bohemond received Taranto and much of the heel of Italy as compensation for losing the Duchy of Apulia and Calabria to his half-brother Roger Borsa. Bohemond soon left on the First Crusade and founded the Principality of Antioch.
principality-of-taranto.r: Taranto became a fief within the Kingdom of Sicily and then the Kingdom of Naples, often granted to royal relatives, such as the Angevin Philip I of Taranto from 1294. Its princes controlled the ports and olive and grain lands of Apulia and could field large armies. Under the Orsini del Balzo in the 15th century it covered much of southern Apulia.
principality-of-taranto.e: Prince Giovanni Antonio Orsini del Balzo, who rebelled against King Ferrante, died in 1463 without legitimate heirs. Ferrante seized his lands, and the principality was absorbed into the royal domain of the Kingdom of Naples.

principality-of-kastrioti.t: Central Albanian lordship of the Kastrioti family, the base from which Gjergj Kastrioti, Skanderbeg, launched his revolt against the Ottomans.
principality-of-kastrioti.o: The Kastrioti family appears in the late 14th century, when Pal Kastrioti held two villages including Sinë, in the Dibër region. His son Gjon Kastrioti built a lordship stretching from the Mat valley towards the Adriatic coast near Lezhë, accepting Ottoman overlordship after the 1380s while trading with Venice and Ragusa.
principality-of-kastrioti.r: Gjon ruled as a regional lord, balancing Ottoman vassalage with Venetian and Ragusan ties; he was made a citizen of Venice and granted trading rights. As the price of submission he sent his sons to the Ottoman court as hostages, among them Gjergj, who was raised a Muslim and served the sultan as a commander.
principality-of-kastrioti.e: After Gjon's death in 1437 the Ottomans absorbed his lands. In 1443 Gjergj, now called Skanderbeg, deserted the Ottoman army after the battle of Niš, seized Krujë and returned to Christianity. In 1444 he gathered the Albanian nobles in the League of Lezhë, which inherited the Kastrioti lordship.

prince-bishopric-of-lubeck.t: The only prince-bishopric to survive the Reformation in Protestant hands, ruled from Eutin by Holstein-Gottorp princes until secularised in 1803.
prince-bishopric-of-lubeck.o: Henry the Lion moved the bishopric of Oldenburg in Holstein to the new town of Lübeck in 1160, and the bishops gathered estates in eastern Holstein. After Henry's fall in 1180 they held these lands as imperial princes. Conflicts with the citizens of the Free and Hanseatic City of Lübeck led them to govern from Eutin.
prince-bishopric-of-lubeck.r: The territory was a small rural principality of lakes and estates around Eutin. After the Reformation the cathedral chapter turned Lutheran and from 1586 elected princes of the house of Holstein-Gottorp, an arrangement the Peace of Westphalia protected. One of them, Adolf Frederick, became King of Sweden in 1751. Eutin grew into a small court town of the Enlightenment, later called the Weimar of the North.
prince-bishopric-of-lubeck.e: In 1803 the see was secularised as the Principality of Lübeck and joined to the Duchy of Oldenburg, whose ruler had been its last prince-bishop. It stayed Oldenburg's exclave until the Greater Hamburg Act of 1937 merged it into Prussian Schleswig-Holstein.

principality-of-waldeck.t: Small north Hessian state of the counts and princes of Waldeck, known for hiring out soldiers and for surviving as a German state until 1918.
principality-of-waldeck.o: The counts of Schwalenberg acquired Waldeck castle above the Eder in the 12th century and took its name, emerging as counts of Waldeck by about 1180. They built up a county in the uplands between Hesse and Westphalia, often under Hessian pressure, and adopted the Reformation in the 16th century. In 1625 they inherited the County of Pyrmont.
principality-of-waldeck.r: The counts, raised to princes in 1712, ruled a poor, rural land of small towns from Arolsen, where they built a baroque palace. Revenue came partly from hiring out regiments to the Dutch Republic and to Britain, including troops used in the American Revolutionary War. George Frederick of Waldeck served as a Dutch field marshal under William III.
principality-of-waldeck.e: Waldeck joined the North German Confederation and in 1868 handed its administration to Prussia while keeping its prince. The last prince abdicated in 1918; the Free State of Waldeck lost Pyrmont in 1922 and merged into Prussia in 1929. The area is now part of Hesse.

populonia.t: The only major Etruscan city on the sea, and the iron-smelting centre of ancient Italy, working ore shipped from the island of Elba.
populonia.o: Populonia, Etruscan Pupluna or Fufluna, stood on the Piombino promontory facing Elba. Villanovan settlements appeared there in the 9th century BCE, and by the 7th century princely tumulus tombs in the San Cerbone necropolis show a powerful elite. Ancient writers disagreed over whether it was founded by Corsicans or by Volaterrae.
populonia.r: Populonia's economy rested on metals: copper and tin from the Campigliese and, from the 6th century BCE, iron ore from Elba smelted in furnaces around the Gulf of Baratti, whose slag heaps later buried the tombs. It was among the first Etruscan cities to mint coins, in the 5th century BCE, often showing the smith god Sethlans or a Gorgon head, and its port linked Etruria to Corsica and Massalia.
populonia.e: Populonia became a Roman ally in the 3rd century BCE and in 205 BCE supplied iron for Scipio's fleet against Carthage. Sacked by Sulla during the civil wars of the 80s BCE, it declined; Strabo found it largely deserted. The slag heaps were mined again for iron in the 20th century, uncovering the necropolis.

powys-wenwynwyn.t: The southern half of Powys, ruled from Welshpool by princes who often sided with England against Gwynedd.
powys-wenwynwyn.o: After Madog ap Maredudd's death in 1160, his nephew Owain Cyfeiliog took the southern part of Powys. It was named after Owain's son Gwenwynwyn ab Owain, who ruled from 1195 and tried to lead the Welsh princes himself.
powys-wenwynwyn.r: Gwenwynwyn's rivalry with Llywelyn the Great of Gwynedd cost him his lands for long periods. His son Gruffydd ap Gwenwynwyn fought and allied with Llywelyn ap Gruffudd in turn, and plotted against him in 1274. Owain Cyfeiliog was a noted poet and founded Strata Marcella Abbey. Welshpool and Powis Castle were its centres.
powys-wenwynwyn.e: Gruffydd supported Edward I in the conquest of 1282 to 1283, and his son Owain surrendered the princely title, holding the lands as an English barony. The heiress married John Charlton, and the lordship of Powis passed to his family.

prince-bishopric-of-utrecht.t: The Sticht, a church principality covering much of the northern Netherlands, whose bishops fought Holland and Guelders for five centuries.
prince-bishopric-of-utrecht.o: Utrecht had been the seat of Willibrord's mission to the Frisians since the late 7th century. In the early 11th century the Salian emperors granted Bishop Adalbold and his successors counties and secular rights, including lands in Drenthe and along the IJssel, turning the see into a principality of the Holy Roman Empire.
prince-bishopric-of-utrecht.r: The territory had two parts: the Nedersticht around Utrecht and the Oversticht, today Overijssel and Drenthe. Utrecht was an imperial favourite, where Conrad II and Henry V died. The bishops were elected by chapters but often imposed by neighbours: David of Burgundy, son of Philip the Good, held the see from 1456. Towns such as Deventer and Kampen grew rich in the Hanseatic trade.
prince-bishopric-of-utrecht.e: Weakened by wars with Holland and the Duchy of Guelders, Bishop Henry of Bavaria transferred his temporal power to Charles V in 1528. The lands became the Lordship of Utrecht and Lordship of Overijssel in the Habsburg Netherlands.

principality-of-monaco.t: A rock on the Riviera seized by the Grimaldis in 1297 and still ruled by them, now one of the world's smallest and richest sovereign states.
principality-of-monaco.o: In January 1297 François Grimaldi, a Genoese Guelph exile, took the fortress of Monaco disguised as a Franciscan friar, an event recalled in the monk on the family arms. The Grimaldis lost and regained the rock several times before establishing lasting control in the 15th century.
principality-of-monaco.r: The Grimaldis governed as lords, later princes, balancing between Genoa, Spain, France and Savoy. Honoré II placed Monaco under French protection in 1641 and adopted the title of prince. Revenues came from tolls, olive oil and citrus from Menton and Roquebrune, until Charles III founded the Monte Carlo casino in 1863.
principality-of-monaco.e: Monaco was annexed by France in 1793 and restored in 1814 under Sardinian protection. Menton and Roquebrune broke away in 1848 and were sold to France in 1861. Constitutions of 1911 and 1962 limited princely power; under Rainier III and Albert II it became a banking and tourism centre.

principality-of-castiglione.t: A small Lombard state of a Gonzaga branch, birthplace of Saint Aloysius Gonzaga, who gave up its succession to become a Jesuit.
principality-of-castiglione.o: Castiglione delle Stiviere, south of Lake Garda, belonged to a cadet branch of the Gonzaga of Mantua. Ferrante Gonzaga, its lord, was made marquis by the emperor in 1579, and the state became a principality under his grandson Francesco in the early 17th century.
principality-of-castiglione.r: The rulers governed a few small towns and farmland as an imperial fief. Ferrante's eldest son Aloysius, born in 1568, renounced his rights to join the Jesuits and died in 1591 nursing plague victims in Rome; he was canonised in 1726 and the town became a pilgrimage centre. His brother Rodolfo was murdered in 1593 by his own subjects. Later princes faced revolts and imperial intervention.
principality-of-castiglione.e: Prince Ferdinando II was deposed after local unrest, and Austrian troops occupied the state in 1691. After long disputes over compensation for the family, the principality was finally incorporated into Austrian Lombardy in 1773.

phaistos.t: Greek city-state built on the ruins of the Minoan palace in southern Crete, rival of Gortyn until destroyed by it c. 150 BCE.
phaistos.o: After the Bronze Age palace fell, Phaistos survived as a settlement on its ridge above the Mesara plain. In the early Iron Age Dorian-speaking Greeks dominated it, and by the Archaic period it was an independent polis, one of many on Crete, with Greek temples built over parts of the old palace.
phaistos.r: Phaistos controlled the western Mesara and the harbour of Matala. It minted coins from the 4th century BCE showing Talos, the bronze giant of myth, and Heracles. Like other Cretan cities it had an aristocratic constitution with kosmoi magistrates and men's messes. Its great rival was Gortyn, a few kilometres east.
phaistos.e: Phaistos was destroyed by Gortyn in the mid-2nd century BCE and its territory absorbed. The site was later known chiefly for its Minoan palace, described separately as the Palace State of Phaistos.

prince-bishopric-of-toul.t: The smallest of the Three Bishoprics of Lorraine, an ecclesiastical principality of the Empire that produced a reforming pope and was absorbed by France.
prince-bishopric-of-toul.o: Toul had been a bishopric since late Roman times. In the 10th century, as the German kings sought loyal counterweights to the Lorraine nobility, the bishops received comital rights over the city and its surroundings, traditionally dated to 928 under Henry the Fowler, making them princes of the Holy Roman Empire.
prince-bishopric-of-toul.r: The bishops ruled a small territory on the upper Moselle, often clashing with the dukes of Lorraine and with the citizens of Toul, who won considerable self-government. Bishop Bruno of Egisheim became Pope Leo IX in 1049 and drove the Gregorian reform. The diocese itself was far larger than the temporal principality.
prince-bishopric-of-toul.e: In 1552 Henry II of France occupied Toul, Metz and Verdun as 'protector' during his war with Charles V. French control of the Three Bishoprics was confirmed by the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, and Toul became part of the Kingdom of France.

paemani.t: One of the Germani Cisrhenani of the Belgian Ardennes, remembered in the name of the Famenne region.
paemani.o: Caesar lists the Paemani with the Condrusi, Eburones and Caeroesi as Germani living west of the Rhine. Their name is usually linked to the Famenne, in the modern Belgian provinces of Namur and Luxembourg.
paemani.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or settlements.
paemani.e: They joined the Belgic coalition against Caesar in 57 BCE. After the conquest they disappear from the sources, their land absorbed into the civitas of the Tungri.

principality-of-anhalt-kothen.t: One of the Anhalt principalities of central Germany, home of the Fruitbearing Society and of the court where Johann Sebastian Bach wrote much of his instrumental music.
principality-of-anhalt-kothen.o: Anhalt was partitioned in 1603 among the sons of Prince Joachim Ernst, and Köthen fell to Ludwig, who founded the line of Anhalt-Köthen. Ludwig was a learned prince who in 1617 co-founded the Fruitbearing Society (Fruchtbringende Gesellschaft), the first society devoted to refining the German language.
principality-of-anhalt-kothen.r: The principality was a small Calvinist state in the Saale-Elbe region, living from agriculture. Its court is best known for Prince Leopold, a music lover who employed Johann Sebastian Bach as Kapellmeister from 1717 to 1723, when the Brandenburg Concertos and much chamber music were composed. In 1665 the line of Anhalt-Plötzkau inherited Köthen, continuing it under a new branch.
principality-of-anhalt-kothen.e: Köthen became a duchy in 1807 under Napoleon's patronage and joined the German Confederation. When its last duke died without heirs in 1847, the territory passed to Anhalt-Dessau and Anhalt-Bernburg, and was absorbed into the united Duchy of Anhalt by 1863.

prince-archbishopric-of-bremen.t: Archbishopric of the North Sea coast, heir to Ansgar's mission to Scandinavia, which ruled the land between the Weser and Elbe until Sweden took it in 1648.
prince-archbishopric-of-bremen.o: The archdiocese of Hamburg was founded in 831 for Ansgar, apostle of the North, and joined to Bremen after Vikings sacked Hamburg in 845. Under Archbishop Adalbert in the 11th century it claimed authority over all of Scandinavia. After Henry the Lion fell in 1180 the archbishops built a secular principality between the lower Weser and Elbe.
prince-archbishopric-of-bremen.r: The archbishops governed marshland and moor from Stade and Bremervörde, while the wealthy city of Bremen slipped from their control. Free peasant communities in the marshes resisted lordship. The estates, including the cathedral chapter, nobles and towns, shared power. In the 16th century the land became Lutheran, and administrators came from princely houses such as Holstein-Gottorp and Denmark.
prince-archbishopric-of-bremen.e: The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 secularised it as the Duchy of Bremen under Sweden, which ruled it with Verden. Denmark took it in 1712 and sold it to the Electorate of Hanover in 1715. The land is now in Lower Saxony.

principality-of-benevento-1806-1815.t: A papal enclave in southern Italy that Napoleon turned into a sovereign principality for his foreign minister Talleyrand.
principality-of-benevento-1806-1815.o: Benevento, a small city surrounded by the Kingdom of Naples, had belonged to the Papal States since the 11th century. In 1806 Napoleon seized it and made Charles-Maurice de Talleyrand, his foreign minister, sovereign Prince of Benevento.
principality-of-benevento-1806-1815.r: Talleyrand never visited his principality. He ruled through a governor, Louis de Beer, who introduced French-style administration and the Napoleonic Code, abolished feudal privileges and improved roads and finances. The small state continued to depend on the Napoleonic Kingdom of Naples (1806–1815) around it.
principality-of-benevento-1806-1815.e: With Napoleon's fall, Talleyrand gave up the title, and the Congress of Vienna returned Benevento to the Papal States in 1815. It remained papal until 1860.

prince-bishopric-of-freising.t: The Bavarian church state of Saint Corbinian, a small principality on the Isar with scattered estates reaching into Austria and Carniola.
prince-bishopric-of-freising.o: The diocese goes back to Saint Corbinian, who worked at Freising around 720, and was formally organised by Saint Boniface in 739. Over the following centuries the bishops gathered estates across Bavaria, Austria, Tyrol and Carniola. Their territory as an imperial principality took shape around the city and the county of Werdenfels, bought in 1294.
prince-bishopric-of-freising.r: The bishop, elected by the cathedral chapter, ruled as a prince of the Holy Roman Empire, but his small core lands were surrounded by Bavaria and he depended heavily on the Wittelsbach dukes, several of whose sons held the see. Freising's cathedral hill was a centre of learning, and the nearby abbey of Weihenstephan brewed beer. The territory remained Catholic.
prince-bishopric-of-freising.e: In 1802 and 1803 the prince-bishopric was secularised and its lands passed to the Electorate of Bavaria, while estates in Austria went to the Habsburgs. The see moved to Munich in 1821 as the Archdiocese of Munich and Freising.

principality-of-anhalt-plotzkau.t: Short-lived Anhalt principality, a minor appanage whose line went on to rule Anhalt-Köthen.
principality-of-anhalt-plotzkau.o: Plötzkau, a small castle district on the Saale, was assigned in the 1603 partition of Anhalt to August, a younger son of Joachim Ernst. It began as an appanage of limited territory rather than a full share, and was formally set up as a principality in 1611.
principality-of-anhalt-plotzkau.r: Little distinguishes its government from the other Anhalt states: it was a small Calvinist territory administered from Plötzkau castle, with revenues from farming along the Saale. Its prince August acted as regent for the young princes of Anhalt-Köthen and served the joint interests of the Anhalt house during the Thirty Years' War.
principality-of-anhalt-plotzkau.e: In 1665 the Köthen line died out and Lebrecht and Emanuel of Anhalt-Plötzkau inherited Anhalt-Köthen, giving up Plötzkau, which returned to Anhalt-Bernburg. The Plötzkau branch thus continued as the ruling house of Köthen until 1847.

prince-bishopric-of-munster.t: The largest church state in the Holy Roman Empire, scene of the Anabaptist kingdom of 1534 and of the peace talks that ended the Thirty Years War.
prince-bishopric-of-munster.o: The Frisian missionary Liudger founded a monastery at Mimigernaford around 793 and became the first bishop of Münster in 805. The bishops acquired counties across Westphalia, and after Henry the Lion fell in 1180 they ruled as imperial princes. Their lands later stretched from the Lippe to the Ems and beyond to the Dutch border.
prince-bishopric-of-munster.r: The cathedral chapter and estates kept a strong voice beside the bishop. In 1534 to 1535 radical Anabaptists under Jan van Leiden turned the city into a theocratic kingdom until Bishop Franz von Waldeck retook it after a siege. The territory remained firmly Catholic. Christoph Bernhard von Galen waged wars against the Dutch Republic, and in the 18th century the minister Franz von Fürstenberg reformed schools and founded the university.
prince-bishopric-of-munster.e: The Peace of Westphalia was negotiated partly in Münster in 1648. The see was secularised in 1802 to 1803 and divided, with the largest share going to Prussia and smaller parts to Oldenburg, Salm and Arenberg. Münster became capital of the Prussian Province of Westphalia.

palace-state-of-knossos.t: The largest Minoan palace centre and later a Mycenaean-ruled capital whose Linear B tablets are the earliest written Greek from Crete.
palace-state-of-knossos.o: Knossos, near modern Heraklion, was occupied from the Neolithic and became Crete's largest settlement. Around 1950 BCE the first palace was built around a central court. Rebuilt after an earthquake c. 1700 BCE, it grew into a complex of more than a thousand rooms, with a town of perhaps several thousand people around it.
palace-state-of-knossos.r: Knossos was the centre of Minoan civilisation, with frescoes such as the bull-leaping scene, light wells, storerooms of pithoi and a theatral area. Administration used Linear A. After c. 1450 BCE Greek-speaking rulers took control and kept records in Linear B, listing sheep, wool, textiles and offerings to gods such as Potnia. The palace then dominated much of central and western Crete.
palace-state-of-knossos.e: The palace was destroyed by fire, traditionally c. 1375 BCE, though the date is debated and some scholars place the final destruction later. Knossos survived as a town and became the Greek city-state described separately as Knossos. Arthur Evans excavated and partly reconstructed the site from 1900.
palace-state-of-knossos.re: Minoan religion; later Mycenaean Greek religion

principality-of-hersfeld.t: A Benedictine abbey in Hesse founded by a disciple of Saint Boniface, whose abbots ruled a principality until it became part of Hesse-Kassel.
principality-of-hersfeld.o: Hersfeld began as a hermitage of Saint Sturmi around 736 and was refounded as a Benedictine monastery by Archbishop Lullus of Mainz around 769. Charlemagne granted it royal protection in 775, making it an imperial abbey. Its relics of Saint Wigbert made it an important pilgrimage centre.
principality-of-hersfeld.r: Hersfeld held lands across Hesse and Thuringia, recorded in the Breviarium Lulli. Its scholars included the chronicler Lambert of Hersfeld, who wrote a major account of the reign of Henry IV. The abbots were princes of the Empire, but rivalry with the town of Hersfeld and with the landgraves of Hesse slowly weakened them.
principality-of-hersfeld.e: The landgraves of Hesse became protectors of the abbey and, after the Reformation, effectively controlled it. In 1648 the Peace of Westphalia secularised Hersfeld as a principality granted to Hesse-Kassel. The ruins of its Romanesque abbey church are among the largest in Germany.

piedmontese-republic.t: The provisional republic set up in Piedmont after the French forced King Charles Emmanuel IV to abandon the mainland in 1798.
piedmontese-republic.o: In December 1798 French troops occupied Turin and forced Charles Emmanuel IV of the Kingdom of Sardinia to give up his mainland states and withdraw to the island of Sardinia. A provisional government of Piedmontese patriots took over in Turin, proclaiming a republic.
piedmontese-republic.r: The provisional government abolished feudal rights and noble titles and held votes in which the Piedmontese communities asked to be annexed to France; the French Directory approved the annexation in early 1799. Real power lay with French commissioners and generals, and French requisitions caused unrest in the countryside.
piedmontese-republic.e: In 1799 the Austro-Russian army under Suvorov drove the French out of Piedmont, ending the regime. After Napoleon's victory at Marengo in 1800, the French set up the Subalpine Republic.

peloponnesian-league.t: Sparta's network of alliances, the leading military coalition of classical Greece and Athens' opponent in the Peloponnesian War.
peloponnesian-league.o: The league grew in the mid-6th century BCE when Sparta, after defeating Tegea around 550 BCE, turned from conquest to alliance. City by city, Peloponnesian states such as Tegea, Corinth, Elis and later Megara swore to have the same friends and enemies as the Lacedaemonians and to follow them wherever they led.
peloponnesian-league.r: There was no common treasury or capital beyond Sparta. Each ally was bound to Sparta by its own treaty; from the late 6th century a congress of allies voted on war, each city having one vote, and Sparta commanded the joint army. Sparta favoured friendly oligarchies in member cities. The league formed the core of Greek resistance to Persia in 480-479 BCE.
peloponnesian-league.e: It fought and won the Peloponnesian War against the Delian League (431-404 BCE), but the Theban victory at Leuctra in 371 BCE and invasions of Laconia broke Sparta's hold. The liberation of Messenia and separate peace deals by Corinth and others in 366-365 BCE ended the league.

paros.t: Cycladic island famed for its fine white marble and its poet Archilochus, and coloniser of Thasos.
paros.o: Paros, in the central Cyclades, was settled by Ionian Greeks in the early Iron Age. Its translucent marble, quarried in underground galleries, became the prized stone of Greek sculptors. By the 7th century BCE Paros was strong enough to colonise Thasos c. 680 BCE and later Parion on the Hellespont.
paros.r: Archilochus, a pioneering lyric and iambic poet, was a Parian who joined the settlement of Thasos. Paros was a commercial and religious centre with a temple of Demeter. It supported Persia in 490 BCE, and the Athenian Miltiades failed to take it in 489 BCE. In the Delian League Paros paid one of the largest island tributes.
paros.e: Paros came under Hellenistic kings and later Roman control by 146 BCE. Its inscribed Parian Chronicle of 264 BCE, now in Oxford, is a key source for Greek chronology, and Parian marble remained in demand.

petrocorii.t: Gallic people of the Dordogne whose name lives on in the Périgord and whose town Vesunna became Périgueux.
petrocorii.o: The Petrocorii lived in the valleys of the Isle and the Dordogne, in the modern Dordogne. Their name is usually read as the four armies, perhaps a league of four communities. Strabo notes their iron workings.
petrocorii.r: Little is known of their rulers. Their main oppidum stood at La Curade near Périgueux.
petrocorii.e: They sent five thousand men to relieve Alesia in 52 BCE. Under Rome their capital was Vesunna, a well-preserved town whose temple tower, the Tour de Vésone, still stands. The city became Périgueux, and the medieval County of Périgord kept their name.

principality-of-schwarzenberg.t: Franconian territory of the Schwarzenberg family, whose princes became some of the greatest landowners and statesmen of the Habsburg monarchy.
principality-of-schwarzenberg.o: The lords of Seinsheim took the name Schwarzenberg from a castle near Scheinfeld in Franconia in the 15th century. In 1599 the family was raised to the rank of imperial counts, and in 1670 Johann Adolf von Schwarzenberg, a senior adviser of Emperor Leopold I, was made a prince of the Empire, with the lands around Scheinfeld forming the core of the family's immediate territory.
principality-of-schwarzenberg.r: The Franconian lands were small, but the family's real weight lay in service to the Habsburgs and in vast estates acquired in Bohemia, including Krumau (Český Krumlov) and Frauenberg (Hluboká), inherited from the Eggenberg family in 1719. The territory was Catholic and administered by officials while the princes lived at court in Vienna or on their Bohemian estates.
principality-of-schwarzenberg.e: In 1806 the Franconian lands were mediatised and placed under the Kingdom of Bavaria. The family remained prominent: Karl Philipp zu Schwarzenberg commanded the allied armies at Leipzig in 1813, and Felix zu Schwarzenberg led the Austrian Empire's government after the 1848 revolution.

political-committee-of-national-liberati.t: The 'Mountain Government' created by the Greek resistance in 1944, which held the first Greek elections in which women voted.
political-committee-of-national-liberati.o: By 1944 the left-wing resistance movement EAM and its army ELAS controlled much of mountainous Greece. On 10 March 1944 EAM created the Political Committee of National Liberation (PEEA) at Viniani in Evrytania, as a rival to both the collaborationist Hellenic State and the government-in-exile in Cairo.
political-committee-of-national-liberati.r: PEEA was led first by Colonel Evripidis Bakirtzis and then by the law professor Alexandros Svolos. It organised local self-government, people's courts and schools in liberated areas, and in April 1944 held elections for a National Council, which met at Koryschades; women voted for the first time in Greece. The Greek forces in Egypt mutinied in its support.
political-committee-of-national-liberati.e: At the Lebanon Conference in May 1944, PEEA agreed to join a government of national unity under Georgios Papandreou, and its ministers entered that government in September. It dissolved after liberation in November 1944, shortly before fighting in Athens began.

principality-of-wales.t: The Welsh state built by the princes of Gwynedd and recognised by England in 1267, the high point of native Welsh political independence.
principality-of-wales.o: Llywelyn ap Iorwerth, Llywelyn the Great, made Gwynedd dominant in Wales, and at Aberdyfi in 1216 the other Welsh rulers accepted his overlordship. His grandson Llywelyn ap Gruffudd took the title Prince of Wales, which Henry III recognised in the Treaty of Montgomery in 1267.
principality-of-wales.r: The principality was a feudal overlordship over lesser Welsh lords such as those of Powys Fadog and Powys Wenwynwyn. Its princes ruled from Gwynedd's courts, including Aber Garth Celyn, and used Welsh law, stone castles such as Dolwyddelan and a growing chancery.
principality-of-wales.e: Llywelyn's refusal to do homage to Edward I led to wars in 1277 and 1282. He was killed near Cilmeri in 1282, and his brother Dafydd executed in 1283. The Statute of Rhuddlan of 1284 annexed the principality to the Kingdom of England.

prince-bishopric-of-verden.t: Small church principality between the Weser and Elbe, rooted in Charlemagne's conquest of the Saxons and handed to Sweden in 1648.
prince-bishopric-of-verden.o: The diocese of Verden was founded around 800 in the wake of Charlemagne's wars against the Saxons. Its bishops acquired estates on the Aller and the lower Weser. After the fall of Henry the Lion in 1180 they ruled a secular territory as imperial princes, though their cathedral city of Verden was largely self-governing and they resided at Rotenburg.
prince-bishopric-of-verden.r: The territory was a thinly settled land of heath and moor. Its bishops were usually drawn from the princely houses of northern Germany, especially Brunswick-Lüneburg. The Reformation spread in the 16th century, and Lutheran administrators such as Philip Sigismund of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel replaced Catholic bishops. In the Thirty Years War the see was held by the Danish prince Frederick, later Frederick III of Denmark.
prince-bishopric-of-verden.e: The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 secularised the see as the Duchy of Verden and gave it to Sweden, which ruled it with Bremen. Denmark seized it in 1712 and sold it to the Electorate of Hanover in 1715. It is now in Lower Saxony.

principality-of-dukagjini.t: Northern Albanian lordship of the Dukagjini family, whose name survives in the customary law code known as the Kanun of Lekë Dukagjini.
principality-of-dukagjini.o: The Dukagjini were a noble family of the northern Albanian highlands who emerged as regional lords in the late 14th century. Around 1387 they held the port of Lezhë and its hinterland, between the territories of the Balšić lords of Zeta and the Kastrioti. Pressed by the Ottomans, they handed Lezhë to Venice in 1393.
principality-of-dukagjini.r: Power rested on control of mountain clans between the Drin river and the plains of Kosovo, with the family dividing lands among branches. The lords switched between Ottoman vassalage and Venetian protection, and were Catholic Christians linked to the bishoprics of the region. Highland society was governed by unwritten custom, later codified under the name of Lekë Dukagjini.
principality-of-dukagjini.e: In 1444 Pal and Lekë Dukagjini joined Skanderbeg's League of Lezhë, folding the lordship into the wider Albanian resistance. Lekë Dukagjini fought on after Skanderbeg's death until the Ottoman conquest of the late 1470s. The Dukagjini plateau and the Kanun still bear the family's name.
